Difficulty rises to medium only if the private-list contention fallback is needed, and to high for the structurally clean per-scan-strategy redesign recorded as the alternative.
improvements.effect_range: Direct A/B: removing the amplification takes CUBRID from 458,209 to 158,930 physical page reads per statement, i.e. -4.57 GiB of page-cache traffic. If the kernel read band scales with bytes, the 2.543 core-s band falls to about 0.882 core-s, releasing roughly 1.66 core-s of the 14.023 core-s Q06 CPU excess (11.8%). That is also 66% of CUBRID's measured 2.500 core-s parallel CPU inflation (20.629 core-s serial -> 23.128 core-s at 6 units), which is the independent upper bound. No wall claim is made beyond that: at 5.97 active units a CPU saving converts to wall only in proportion to utilization, so the expected wall gain is about 0.28 s of 3.875 s. On a host where the data did NOT fit the OS page cache the same 4.57 GiB would be device I/O and the effect would be far larger; this campaign's host makes Q06 the CHEAP case, not the expensive one.
improvements.evidence_event: physical page reads per statement for one full scan of the same relation in the same pool, as a function of nothing but the number of scan units. Denominator: lineitem = 682,937 CUBRID heap pages of 16 KiB in a 524,288-page (8 GiB) pool, so the arithmetically unavoidable overflow is 682,937 - 524,288 = 158,649 pages per statement. Measured by /proc/<cub_server>/io syscr deltas divided by the statement count, cross-checked against the trace's own ioread counter.
improvements.explanation: One scan thread reads 158,930 pages per statement - the predicted overflow to within 0.18% - so CUBRID's replacement policy retains the entire pool's worth of the relation and behaves optimally. The identical scan on 3, 6 or 12 pooled workers reads 468,980 / 458,209 / 459,242 pages, retaining only 213,957-224,728, and the degradation is flat in DOP rather than proportional to it: it is a step change caused by WHICH LRU list receives the pages, not by concurrency pressure. PostgreSQL, whose scan-resistance is a per-scan strategy ring rather than a per-thread list, reads 76,987 pages serially and 78,482 at DOP 5 against a predicted overflow of 76,552 - a 1.9% DOP effect against CUBRID's 188%.
improvements.implementation_direction: Propagate the parent's LRU identity into the parallel-scan worker's thread entry at src/query/parallel/px_scan/px_scan_task.cpp:94, next to the existing m_px_orig_thread_entry assignment: copy m_parent_thread_p->private_lru_index and call pgbuf_thread_variables_init() so m_is_private_lru_enabled follows, and clear both again on retire (thread_entry_task.cpp:75-76 already does). All N workers of one scan then share the ONE private list of the session that owns the query, which is the same list the serial path uses, so the serial retention behaviour is reproduced exactly rather than approximated. Cheaper and less invasive alternative if sharing one private list across workers proves contended: keep the shared list but insert scan pages at the TOP rather than the MIDDLE when the fixing thread is a parallel-scan worker of a sequential scan; that recovers most of the retention without touching thread identity. The structurally cleanest fix - and the one PostgreSQL's design argues for - is to make scan-resistance a property of the SCAN (a per-scan ring/strategy handed to pgbuf_fix, as in freelist.c:426) instead of a property of the fixing thread, which removes the whole class of defect rather than this instance.

The mechanism claim therefore rests on (a) the source branch at page_buffer.c:6900-6934 together with thread_entry_task.cpp:75-76,95 and px_scan_task.cpp:94, and (b) the measurement being a STEP at >=2 workers that is then flat across DOP 3, 6 and 12 rather than scaling with worker count. A contention explanation predicts DOP dependence and is rejected by that flatness; it is not excluded by a single-worker control, and that gap is recorded rather than glossed. The validation criteria above are written so that applying the fix settles it either way.
measurement.pool_state_dependence: The parallel read count is itself unstable across pool states while the serial one is not: the three headline-regime telemetry blocks all measured 608,510 reads per statement (rchar 39,874,595,032-096 bytes per 4-statement block, i.e. 89.1% miss) while the lru_ab probe, which drives each variant to its own equilibrium with two extra passes first, measured 458,209-468,980 across DOP 3/6/12 (67.1-68.7%). Serial measured 158,930 and 162,257 in the same two settings (23.27% and 23.76%). Read amplification is therefore 2.88x-3.83x depending on pool state, and the section 12 headline regime sits at the 3.83x end. That the PARALLEL figure wobbles by 33% while the SERIAL figure is pinned to the arithmetic overflow is additional evidence that the parallel path's retention is unstable, not merely lower.

q_evidence.Q12: Q12 extends IMP-010 from SELF-eviction to COLLATERAL eviction, which is a qualitatively new consequence of the same root cause. Q06 measured the parallel scan re-reading the relation IT WAS SCANNING; Q12 measures it evicting a DIFFERENT relation -- the inner side of its own index-nested-loop join. Direct same-engine A/B on one traced statement each, /proc/<cub_server>/io bracketed: PARALLEL 613,666 read syscalls and 9.361 GiB, SERIAL /*+ NO_PARALLEL_SCAN */ 418,246 and 6.376 GiB -- the parallel path adds 195,420 reads and 2.985 GiB per statement (+46.7%), cross-checked by statdump Num_data_page_ioreads 613,460 vs 417,882. The collateral part is the decisive number: CUBRID's trace charges 100,930-117,883 of those reads to the orders PK index+heap SCAN node (two traced runs, pool-state dependent), while PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports 'Index Scan using orders_pkey ... Buffers: shared hit=1109634' with read=0 -- ZERO physical reads on 310,803 probes -- for a near-identical fix count (CUBRID 1,105,561 = 0.9963x of PostgreSQL's 1,109,634). PostgreSQL's BAS_BULKREAD ring (heapam.c:397-410, chosen because lineitem's 1,125,128 blocks exceed NBuffers/4 = 262,144) confines the 8,790 MiB scan to a 256 kB ring per worker so the 2,483 MB orders relation stays fully resident in the same 8192 MB budget; CUBRID's scan pages go through pgbuf_unlatch_void_zone_bcb (page_buffer.c:6845, :6900-6934) into an LRU list with no per-scan strategy, and evict the join's inner side. The addressable CPU on Q12 is bounded: the whole kernel page-cache band is 2.4326 core-s of which only the +0.5360 core-s delta over PostgreSQL's 1.8966 core-s is recoverable, i.e. 7.9% of Q12's 6.7771 core-s excess -- so on Q12 this candidate is real, directly proved, and NOT the dominant term (IMP-020 is, at 69.5%). device read_bytes was 0 on the serial statement and 5,607,424 on the parallel one, so the cost is page-cache re-read CPU, not storage I/O. raw/Q12/q12-serial-parallel.out, q12-serial-serial.out, q12-serial-io-*.txt, q12-serial-statdump-*.txt, q12-plan-act-pg.out, q12-profile-bands.txt.

Against IMP-008's 7.624 core-s (54.4% of the CPU excess) IMP-010 is worth about 1.66 core-s (11.8%), so it loses on magnitude but wins decisively on evidence quality and cost: it is the only Q06 candidate proved by a direct same-engine A/B with an arithmetically predicted control value (158,649 predicted vs 158,930 measured), and its fix is a two-field propagation rather than an executor specialization. Bands are disjoint by symbol from IMP-008 (kernel read path versus predicate/domain evaluation) so their effects add; they are NOT disjoint from IMP-007, which is why that relation is recorded as multiplicative.

relations.alternative: A generic scan-resistance ring handed to pgbuf_fix per scan (the PostgreSQL design at freelist.c:426) instead of per-thread list selection. Recorded as the structurally correct alternative and explicitly NOT costed here.
relations.predecessor: IMP-002 - Q06 does not merely add evidence to IMP-002, it RE-SCOPES it. IMP-002 claims the replacement policy 'fails to retain a working set that marginally exceeds the pool'. Q06's serial control refutes that for the serial path on exactly such a working set (682,937 pages against a 524,288-page pool retains 524,007, the arithmetic optimum), so the failure IMP-002 measured on Q01/Q03/Q04 is localized here to the parallel scan path. IMP-002's Q01/Q03/Q04 evidence was collected on parallel scans and has NOT been re-measured serially, so those relations are flagged for re-validation rather than reassigned.
related: IMP-007 - COMPOSES MULTIPLICATIVELY WITH THIS AND MUST NOT BE SUMMED. IMP-010 sets HOW MANY misses occur (458,209 vs 158,930), IMP-007 sets HOW EACH ONE IS SERVED (a synchronous single-page 16 KiB pread on the query thread). They share the identical 2.543 core-s kernel band, so their joint upper bound is that band, not the sum of two separate claims.

IMP-005 - same subsystem boundary (pooled parallel-scan workers behaving differently from the serial path) and same fix locality (px_scan_task.cpp), but a statistics/observability defect rather than a buffer one; no effect overlap.

improvements.root_cause_title: A heap scan's newly read pages are inserted at the TOP of the session's private LRU list when the scan runs on the client transaction thread, but only into the MIDDLE of a round-robin SHARED LRU list when the same scan runs on pooled parallel-query workers, because a worker's thread entry is recycled with private_lru_index = -1 and the parallel-scan task never propagates its parent's LRU identity - so going parallel silently discards the buffer pool's scan-resistance and re-reads 2.88x the pages
improvements.upstream_precedent: No prior CBRD issue or PR that propagates the session's private LRU index into parallel-scan workers was identified in the pinned tree at 607f1ee9. The pattern of propagating per-session executor state into px workers IS established at px_scan_task.cpp:94 for m_px_orig_thread_entry, so this is an extension of an accepted pattern rather than a new one. On the PostgreSQL side the corresponding change is ancient and settled - BAS_BULKREAD ring buffers for large scans - which is why PostgreSQL's numbers here are DOP-independent; that is a precedent for the design, not for the CUBRID patch.
improvements.validation_criteria: (1) Q01-Q22 results byte-identical - mandatory for any buffer change even though placement cannot affect correctness. (2) Q06 CUBRID physical reads per statement fall from 458,209 to within 5% of the serial 158,930 at DOP 6, measured the same way (/proc/<cub_server>/io syscr delta / statement count) and cross-checked against the trace ioread counter. (3) The measured value stays within 5% of 158,930 at DOP 3 and DOP 12 as well, since DOP independence is the property being restored. (4) The rep_movs_alternative + filemap_* kernel band falls from 11.01% to under 5% of profiled self cost. (5) Q06 CUBRID median wall improves against 3.875 s under the same warm_establish + measure_block protocol with the WARM gate still CONVERGED, and the block-to-block spread does not exceed the 3.08% recorded here. (6) No regression in Q01/Q03/Q04 physical reads - those queries' IMP-002 evidence must be RE-MEASURED with this fix, because Q06 shows their 'pool cannot retain a marginally oversized working set' conclusion may in fact be this defect. (7) A high-DOP contention check: cub_server mutex/latch time on the private list must not rise above its current 3.50% buffer-manager band.

improvements.q08_relation: Q08 is a POSITIVE CONTROL and this candidate is explicitly NOT related to Q08's gap. The same code path picks an index-NL chain on Q08 and that choice is correct: CUBRID's /*+ USE_HASH(orders, customer) */ variant - PostgreSQL's native shape on the dominant path - measures 1.718 s against native 1.136 s (1.5123x slower) at 2.5492x the total query CPU, and PostgreSQL forced onto CUBRID's index-NL shape is 1.0364x FASTER than its own parallel-hash choice (0.986521 s vs 1.022423 s), so Q08's F_plan = 0.964885x. CUBRID's cost model rates the two plans 288,795 vs 3,112,001: the ORDERING is right and the MAGNITUDE is 7.1x pessimistic, which is this candidate's HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT and per-row spill-penalty behaviour costing nothing when the ordering it produces is correct. Q08 therefore supplies the second counterexample this candidate's validation criteria demand (after Q05's native index-NL choice). Note also that Q07's px_scan_checker parallel block did NOT bite on Q08: the driving spec is a 24,353-page part heap scan rather than a 1-page nation scan, so CUBRID does parallelise the chain (parallel workers: 5). The Q08 defect is the DEGREE and the non-participating coordinator, registered separately as IMP-012.
improvements.q09_evidence: Q09: second instance of an index-nested-loop plan being chosen over a hash plan that the same executor runs faster (CUBRID native 10.980999 s vs /*+ USE_HASH(orders, supplier) */ 7.118999 s = 1.5425x), but Q09 REFINES this candidate's scope rather than confirming its mechanism. (a) The parallel-degree-blindness half does not apply: CUBRID's chosen NL plan is parallel (trace 'parallel workers: 5', U=4.97459), and the rejected hash plan reaches U=6.23022 with a 12.1704-unit peak. (b) The HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT anti-hash offset is 1,500 against a plan-cost gap of 984,797-36,082 = 948,715, i.e. 0.16% of the difference, so it is not the deciding term either. On Q09 the deciding term is the join-cardinality input to those same cost functions: IMP-014. Effects must not be summed. raw/Q09/q9-plan-est-cubrid.out, raw/Q09/variants/plan-USE_HASH_ORDERS_SUPPLIER.out, raw/Q09/Q09-cubrid-hashos-headline.json.
improvements.q10_evidence: Q10 is a NEGATIVE control for this candidate, and the strongest one in the campaign so far: on Q10 CUBRID's join-method choice is not merely acceptable, it is BETTER than PostgreSQL's. CUBRID natively picks the index-NL chain (orders sscan -> lineitem fk_lineitem_orders -> customer PK) and its own hash alternative is far worse - /*+ USE_HASH(lineitem, customer) */ measures 13.809 s and 13.869 s against 7.10-7.13 s native (1.94x slower) at an estimated cost of 9,427,968 against 649,494. PostgreSQL, on the same data, chose a Parallel Hash Join tree and is 1.698x SLOWER for it: forcing PostgreSQL onto CUBRID's shape with enable_hashjoin=off, enable_mergejoin=off gives a gated block median of 2.484120 s against 4.218695 s native. So Q10's F_plan on the PostgreSQL-side anchor is 0.588836x, below 1.0, in CUBRID's favour. Any future work on IMP-011 must keep Q10 as a regression control that the fix does not push CUBRID toward the hash plan here.
improvements.q14_evidence: Q14 is this candidate's ISOLATING EXPERIMENT and its cleanest instance so far: it is the first query where the per-row hash SPILL PENALTY alone -- not parallel-degree blindness, not cardinality error, not HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT -- inverts the plan ranking, and the inversion is reproduced arithmetically from the source constants. CUBRID natively picks idx-join (sscan lineitem -> iscan part.pk_part_p_partkey, cost 1,220,202); the hash-join alternative over the SAME two scans costs 2,416,443. The difference is exactly 1,376,016 = (2,000,000 + 752,032) x HJ_FILE_IO_WEIGHT 0.5, i.e. the spill term is 100.0% of the 1,196,241 decision margin. Removing it makes the hash plan win by 179,775, which is precisely what happens when max_hash_list_scan_size is raised to 128M: the optimizer then picks hash-join with NO hint and cost 1,040,427 (q14-plan-est-cubrid-hashmem128.out). MEASUREMENT (three gated section-12 blocks, same engine, same 8-FK schema, same statistics, same parallelism, WARM-proved, all CLEAN on attempt 1): native idx-join 3.228 s; hash-join at the CONTRACT-DEFAULT 8 MB budget via /*+ USE_HASH(part, lineitem) */ 2.880 s; hash-join at 128 MB 2.959 s. The cost model rates native 1.98x CHEAPER than the 8 MB hash plan that is in fact 1.1208x FASTER -- a ranking inversion, not a magnitude error. THE SPILL IS REAL AND NEARLY FREE, which is the specific refinement Q14 contributes. The 8 MB hash run genuinely partitions: q14-trace-cubrid-usehash2.out prints 'SPLIT (time: 89, ..., partitions: 6)' and 'BUILD ... method: hybrid', against 'BUILD ... method: memory' with no SPLIT node at 128 MB. The partition count is predicted exactly by the in-tree formula -- ceil(749,223 x 52 B / (8 MiB x PARTITION_FILL_FACTOR 0.8)) = 6, where 52 B = 2*sizeof(MHT_HLS_SLOT) + sizeof(MHT_HLS_ENTRY) + HJ_HASH_ENTRY_POS_SIZE -- which independently confirms the cost model's own threshold arithmetic. The measured cost of that spill is 89 ms of a 3,244 ms statement (2.7%). Anchoring the cost scale on the native plan (1,220,202 units <-> 3.228 s = 2.6455 us/unit), the 1,376,016-unit penalty implies 3.640 s of wall. The spill is therefore OVERCHARGED BY 40.9x. A PER-PAGE charge, this candidate's proposed fix (a), would bill inner_pages + outer_pages ~ 4,521 units instead of 1,376,016 and the hash plan would win on cost. MEMORY BUDGET REJECTED as the root cause: raising max_hash_list_scan_size does NOT explain the gap, and Q14 measures that directly. The 128 MB single-batch run (2.959 s) is 0.0274x SLOWER than the 8 MB partitioned run (2.880 s), so the budget is not the defect and 'make max_hash_list_scan_size bigger / scale it with data_buffer_size' is a rejected explanation, rejected by 79 ms. The defect is the cost model's valuation of spilling, not the amount of memory. PARALLEL-DEGREE BLINDNESS DOES NOT APPLY on Q14, which refines this candidate's scope the same way Q09 did: CUBRID's chosen idx-join is already parallel (trace 'parallel workers: 6', U=5.96455, TWU=5.9536) and CUBRID's parallelism is the BETTER of the two here -- CUBRID's own NO_PARALLEL_SCAN A/B is 18.012999 s vs 3.228 s = 5.5802x speedup for a 7.00% CPU surcharge (93.6% efficiency against U), while PostgreSQL's max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0 A/B is 6.651414 s vs 1.712645 s = 3.8837x for a 39.05% surcharge (67.2%). F_units on Q14 is 1.001341x. HJ_MEM_ALLOC_CONSTANT is again not the deciding term: 1,500 against a 1,196,241 margin is 0.13%, matching Q09's 0.16% finding. POSITIVE CONTROL FROM THE OTHER ENGINE: PostgreSQL forced onto CUBRID's nested-loop-index shape (enable_hashjoin=off, enable_mergejoin=off) measures 2.086580 s against 1.712645 s native, so the hash shape is worth 1.2183x to PostgreSQL on the same data. Both engines' cost models are asked the same question and only CUBRID's answers wrong. Q14's F_plan = 1.120833x of a 1.884804x total gap; fixing this candidate alone would move Q14's R_wall to 1.681625x.

q_evidence.Q11: Q11 NEGATIVE CONTROL, and a regression control. The one plan decision the two optimizers make differently on Q11 is the aggregation strategy - CUBRID sorts (`GROUPBY ... sort: true`), PostgreSQL hashes (`HashAggregate, Planned Partitions: 16, Batches: 17, Memory Usage: 8337kB, Disk Usage: 15064kB`) - and PostgreSQL's choice is the WRONG one: forcing it onto CUBRID's shape with enable_hashagg=off measures 0.739912 s against 0.798124 s native, so PostgreSQL's own cost model costs it 1.0787x and Q11's F_plan on that anchor is 0.927064x, BELOW 1.0. Both engines' join shapes are otherwise node-for-node identical (nation filter -> supplier via the FK index -> partsupp via fk_partsupp_supplier, 4,049 index searches on each side, both reported by each engine's own instrumentation). Any future IMP-011 work must keep Q11 as a regression control: there is nothing to gain here and a plan-cost change could lose 7.9%.

improvements.explanation: CUBRID derives its parallel degree from the driving relation's page count and then leaves its coordinator idle, so a plan whose per-page work is three orders of magnitude above a bare scan gets 5 executing threads out of a configured 6; PostgreSQL gets 5 workers plus a participating leader on the identical shape, and prices the leader in its cost model.
improvements.implementation_direction: Two independently shippable steps. (a) Let the coordinator execute a task: in manager::next(), when the merged-list read would block and an unclaimed input range remains, run one task inline on the calling thread - the input handler already partitions by range, so no new partitioning is needed, and this is the direct analogue of PostgreSQL's need_to_scan_locally. (b) Make the SCAN auto_degree aware of the per-page work of the scan_ptr chain hanging off the spec rather than of the driving relation's page count alone, and reach the configured parallelism when that work justifies it; the cheapest correct version multiplies num_pages by the estimated inner-probe count already available in the plan the spec came from, keeping plan_generation.c:3204-3234 consistent.
improvements.measurement: F_units = U_P_idxnl / U_C_native = 5.25338 / 3.82408 = 1.373763x. Unit-count component = peak_P / peak_C = 6.2449 / 5.2166 = 1.1971x = 87% of F_units. Remainder 1.1476x = the longer CUBRID serial tail (0.337 s vs 0.232 s) plus a 7.5% straggler spread across the five CUBRID workers (heap time 1018..1094 ms).
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: For a parallel heap scan CUBRID calls compute_parallel_degree(SCAN, num_pages, hint). The SCAN branch computes auto_degree = floor(log2(num_pages / parallel_scan_page_threshold)) + 2 then degree = MIN(auto_degree, parallelism). Q08's driving relation part has 24,353 heap pages and parallel_scan_page_threshold defaults to 2048 (a PRM_HIDDEN parameter), so x = 11, floor(log2 11) = 3, auto_degree = 5 and MIN(5, 6) = 5: the configured parallelism=6 is never reached. The degree is a function of the DRIVING relation's page count alone - it cannot see that each of those pages drives about 16 lineitem index probes plus an orders and a customer PK probe, i.e. that per-page work here is three orders of magnitude above a bare scan. Then manager::start_tasks() pushes exactly m_parallelism tasks to the worker pool and returns; the calling transaction thread's only scan-related work in manager::next() is m_result_handler->read() on the merged list. Active units therefore equal the degree: the coordinator contributes 0.20 core-s of the 4.34 core-s statement and never executes a scan task.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: compute_parallel_worker() also derives workers from a page-count logarithm (log3 ladder on min_parallel_table_scan_size / min_parallel_index_scan_size) but on the same relation returns the full max_parallel_workers_per_gather cap of 5, and then the leader ALSO executes the plan: nodeGatherMerge.c:253-254 'if (parallel_leader_participation || node->nreaders == 0)' and :403-404 'Slot 0 is always for the leader. Leader always calls ExecProcNode()', with nodeGather.c:214-215 doing the same for plain Gather. The cost model knows it - get_parallel_divisor() adds 1.0 - 0.3 * nworkers of leader contribution to the divisor. Measured result: loops=6 on every node under the Gather Merge and peak 6.2449 active units.

improvements.root_cause_title: The parallel-scan coordinator is a pure consumer and the SCAN auto-degree formula saturates below the configured parallelism cap, so a plan CUBRID does parallelise runs at 5 active units where PostgreSQL runs the identical shape at 6 (5 workers plus a participating leader) - the sole factor above 1.0 in Q08's causal card, F_units 1.373763x of a 1.111086x gap
improvements.upstream_precedent: No precedent in the pinned CUBRID history for a participating parallel coordinator. PR #7441, included in this campaign's source SHA 607f1ee9, added parallel hash-join EXECUTION; it did not change start_tasks()'s submit-only model or the SCAN auto-degree formula.
improvements.validation_criteria: Q08 CUBRID peak active units >= 6.0 and U >= 4.5 with no hint, wall within 5% of the projected 0.998 s; Q07's USE_HASH variant U = 7.19707 does not regress; Q05's uncorrelated-subquery degree (IMP-009) is untouched; Q01-Q22 plan-shape diff reviewed and TPC-H SF10 total wall not regressed; the new degree validated against measured U, never against the configured parallelism cap. Step (a) must not ship before IMP-005 is fixed, because it adds another trace-merge level.

improvements.correctness_risk: Low. The LRU boost is a replacement-policy hint with no effect on visibility, latching, logging or recovery. No operator semantics change.

improvements.difficulty_reason: Option (a) is a localized predicate in one function, and pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb's own comment already documents an age-based suppression rule for a neighbouring case, so the precedent for suppressing a boost exists in-file. Options (b) batching and (c) replacing the LRU lists with a clock sweep are medium-high and very high respectively.
improvements.effect_range: Bounded above by the 27.41% + 5.32% band and bounded below by the fact that a clock sweep still pays the locate-and-pin cost. A realistic target is the pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb plus mutex portion, 10.73% of profiled self cost, i.e. about 0.47 core-s of the 4.34 core-s statement, which at the measured U is about 0.12 s of wall. Combined with IMP-012 that puts CUBRID clearly ahead of PostgreSQL's 1.022423 s.
improvements.evidence_event: self cost as a share of resolved perf samples, attached to verified PID sets (CUBRID cub_server pid 1612732 with all 31 query threads inside it; PostgreSQL postmaster attached before the client connected so inherit-on-fork covers the leader and every statement's workers). 0 [unknown] symbol lines and 0 lost samples on both sides: 75,004 CUBRID samples over 20.002 s, 111,037 PostgreSQL samples over 20.002 s. CUBRID pgbuf_fix_release 17.76% + pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb 5.41% + pgbuf_unfix 4.24% = 27.41%, libpthread 5.32%; PostgreSQL PinBuffer 1.91% + LWLockAttemptLock 1.23% + LockBufferInternal 0.56% = 3.70%, libpthread 0.00%. Call graph confirms pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb is reached from heap_get_visible_version -> pgbuf_unfix on the per-row path.
improvements.evidence_type: profile attribution (upper bound on the band). Not a direct A/B: no in-contract switch disables the LRU boost, and changing data_buffer_size would be a measurement-contract change requiring user approval.
improvements.explanation: CUBRID's LRU replacement policy needs list order, so it pays a mutex-protected unlink/relink plus zone rebalance on every unfix of a resident page; PostgreSQL's clock sweep needs no order, so it pays one atomic counter bump - which is why CUBRID's 6.6x smaller tuple-touch count only converts into a 16% CPU advantage instead of a wall win.
improvements.implementation_direction: Three options, cheapest first. (a) Extend the existing age-based suppression: pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb's own comment already documents 'if a page is quickly fixed several times, its age is really small ... we don't boost it', implemented in pgbuf_unlatch_bcb_upon_unfix; a random index-probe workload is the opposite case - a cold SINGLE touch of a zone-2/3 page - which that rule does not cover. Suppress the boost when the BCB's hit count since insertion is 1 and the fix was a read-only visibility fetch. (b) Batch the boost: record boost intent in the BCB and apply it under one mutex acquisition per N unfixes. (c) Replace the LRU lists with a clock sweep over the BCB array, removing the list and the per-list mutex entirely; freelist.c StrategyGetBuffer() is the reference shape.
measurement: F_cost = (CPU_C/W_C)/(CPU_P/W_P) = 1034.2 ns / 194.4 ns = 5.320850x, against F_work = W_C/W_P = 0.151371x, so F_cpu(native) = 0.805422x. CUBRID retires 0.7391x PostgreSQL's instructions (252.359 G vs 341.463 G) at 1.0909x the IPC (1.20 vs 1.10), and switches context 38.5x more often (2.734 K/s vs 71/s).

Q13: first instance of this candidate measured FREE of a miss-count confound. Page fixes at the matched node are equal to 1.000259x (CUBRID trace fetch 19,504,609 vs PostgreSQL Index Scan Buffers: shared hit=19,499,552) and BOTH engines take zero physical reads (/proc read_bytes 0, Num_data_page_ioreads delta 0, blks_read delta 0). For that identical page-fix count CUBRID spends 10.210 core-s per statement (pgbuf_fix_release 13.86%, pgbuf_unfix 3.49%, pgbuf_replace_watcher 1.07%, pgbuf_ordered_fix_release 0.34%, plus 2.31 points of libpthread mutex traffic: __pthread_mutex_trylock 0.98, __pthread_mutex_unlock_usercnt 0.86, __pthread_mutex_lock 0.47) against PostgreSQL's 7.006 core-s (hash_search_with_hash_value 10.19%, PinBuffer 7.74%, LWLockAttemptLock 6.69%, StartReadBuffer 1.13%, LockBufferInternal 1.07%, LWLockRelease 1.06%, GetPrivateRefCountEntrySlow 0.94%, UnpinBufferNoOwner 0.87%, hash_bytes 0.86%, BufferLockUnlock 0.63%, ResourceOwnerForget 0.58%). Ratio 1.4573x, contributing 3.204 core-s = 12.1% of Q13's 26.3964 core-s CPU gap.
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb() is called on unfix of any BCB that lives in LRU zone 2 or 3. It takes pthread_mutex_lock(&lru_list->mutex), calls pgbuf_remove_from_lru_list() to unlink the BCB from its current position, pgbuf_lru_add_bcb_to_top() to relink it at the head, and then pgbuf_lru_adjust_zone1() or pgbuf_lru_adjust_zones(), which walk the list to re-balance zone boundaries through pgbuf_bcb_change_zone(). On Q08's dominant path this runs once PER HEAP ROW: heap_get_visible_version() -> heap_clean_get_context -> pgbuf_unfix -> pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb, verified in the call graph at 5.38% of the parallel-query threads' cost. Q08 performs about 1.35 M fix/unfix pairs per statement (403,487 lineitem + 403,487 orders + 122,404 customer + 24,254 supplier heap lookups, each preceded by its index descent), so the list is reordered under a mutex about a million times per statement on pages that were already resident.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: UnpinBuffer() / UnpinBufferNoOwner() decrement a PROCESS-LOCAL PrivateRefCountEntry->refcount and, only when it reaches zero, issue one pg_atomic_fetch_sub_u64(&buf->state, BUF_REFCOUNT_ONE). PinBuffer() bumps usagecount INSIDE the same compare-and-swap that takes the pin ('Default case: increase usagecount unless already max'). PostgreSQL's replacement algorithm is a clock sweep over the buffer array, so there is no ordered list to maintain, no per-list mutex to acquire and no zone rebalance to run. Searched src/storage/page_buffer.c for clock / sweep / usage_count / usagecount: CUBRID has no clock-sweep equivalent - the file implements private and shared LRU lists with zones 1/2/3.

improvements.priority_justification: Largest single profile band on either engine (27.41% fix/unfix/LRU + 5.32% libpthread) and the direct driver of F_cost = 5.320850x (1034.2 ns vs 194.4 ns of total query CPU per plan-node tuple touch). Ranked below IMP-012 because it is not the factor that loses Q08: F_cpu = 0.838224x already favours CUBRID by 16%.
improvements.q09_evidence: Q09: second measured instance and the largest absolute band of the campaign. pgbuf fix/unfix/LRU/victim = 21.38% of CUBRID's resolved samples (pgbuf_fix_release 11.66%, pgbuf_unfix 3.42%, pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb 1.98%, pgbuf_unlatch_void_zone_bcb 1.71%) plus 5.49% libpthread mutex, against PostgreSQL's 10.03% pin/unpin/clock-sweep/lwlock. In absolute terms 11.68 core-s per CUBRID statement vs 3.07 core-s per PostgreSQL statement. Context switches 284,577 in 25.002 s (2.266 K/s) vs PostgreSQL 14,412 (102.6/s), 22.1x. This is the dominant identified part of the 1.297496x same-shape CPU residual that survives after Q09's plan factor is removed. raw/Q09/profile-cubrid-flat.txt, raw/Q09/profile-pg-flat.txt, raw/Q09/q9-profile-bands.txt, raw/Q09/perf-stat-*.txt.
improvements.q10_evidence: Q10: the largest single CUBRID profile band, and the cleanest cross-engine contrast for this candidate yet. CUBRID spends 14.60% of cycles in pgbuf fix/unfix plus LRU-victim machinery (pgbuf_fix_release 6.17%, pgbuf_get_victim_candidates_from_lru 4.03%, pgbuf_unfix 1.85%, pgbuf_unlatch_void_zone_bcb 0.97%, pgbuf_get_victim_from_lru_list 0.84%, pgbuf_get_victim 0.42%, pgbuf_claim_bcb_for_fix 0.32%) plus 3.35% in libpthread mutexes (__pthread_mutex_lock 1.36%, __pthread_mutex_unlock_usercnt 1.09%, __pthread_mutex_trylock 0.90%) = 17.95% combined, against PostgreSQL's 1.66% for the equivalent function (LWLockAttemptLock 1.04% + PinBuffer 0.62%) - a 10.8x relative share. Context-switch rate from perf stat on the verified PID sets: CUBRID 249,411 in 30.002 s (2.363 K/s) against PostgreSQL 91,164 (751/s), 3.15x. Q10 also isolates the band from plan choice: CUBRID performs 24,556,558 plan-node tuple touches against PostgreSQL's 86,617,111 (F_work 0.283507x, i.e. CUBRID touches 3.53x FEWER tuples) and still spends 1.251216x the total query CPU, giving F_cost 4.413350x - 995.3 ns of total query CPU per tuple touch against 225.5 ns. Instruction counts confirm it is not a stall effect: IPC is 1.59 on BOTH engines, while CUBRID retires 78.06 G instructions per statement against PostgreSQL's 66.76 G.
improvements.q17_counterexample: Q17 is a measured COUNTER-EXAMPLE and deliberately does NOT carry a Q17 q_relation. On Q17's plane-shape-controlled pair PostgreSQL spends 5.8x MORE core-seconds on buffer management than CUBRID: CUBRID's band (pgbuf_fix_release 5.93% + pgbuf_unfix 1.31% + pthread mutex 1.30% = 8.92%) is 0.06413 core-s, while PostgreSQL's (PinBuffer 3.67 + StartReadBuffer 2.83 + GetPrivateRefCountEntrySlow 2.77 + LWLockRelease 2.68 + UnpinBufferNoOwner 2.63 + LWLockAttemptLock 2.55 + LockBufferInternal 2.34 + BufferLockUnlock 2.06 + ResourceOwnerForget 1.74 + hash_search_with_hash_value 8.30 + hash_bytes 2.33 + siblings = 37.99%) is 0.37327 core-s. The cause is workload, not policy: PostgreSQL takes 2,198,652 buffer accesses of which 95.1% (2,090,095) come from 61,385 correlated-SubPlan index scans that CUBRID's subquery memo reduces to 2,044 executions. Recorded so this candidate's effect range is not generalised to plans where CUBRID performs far fewer buffer accesses than PostgreSQL.

q_evidence.Q11: Q11 REFUTES this candidate as a differentiator, and does so under the best possible conditions for it. In the saturated state BOTH engines take zero physical reads, so the buffer bands are pure hit-path cost with no miss confound: CUBRID 21.07% (pgbuf_fix_release 17.06, pgbuf_unfix 2.45, pgbuf_ordered_fix_release 0.71, pgbuf_ordered_unfix 0.47, pgbuf_set_dirty 0.38) plus 3.06% libpthread = 24.13%, against PostgreSQL 23.72% (hash_search_with_hash_value 12.73 - which the call graph resolves to BufTableLookup through StartReadBuffer -> PinBufferForBlock -> BufferAlloc, NOT to the HashAggregate - plus PinBuffer 4.41, LWLockAttemptLock 1.70, LockBufferInternal 0.76, UnpinBufferNoOwner 0.74, GetPrivateRefCountEntrySlow 0.70, LWLockRelease 0.68, StartReadBuffer 0.65, BufferLockUnlock 0.53, hash_bytes 0.47, ResourceOwnerForget 0.35). Shares are equal to 1.017x. Per page fix CUBRID spends 1339.0 ns of TOTAL QUERY CPU against PostgreSQL's 1475.2 ns, i.e. CUBRID is 1.1017x CHEAPER, and CUBRID's IPC is 1.65 against PostgreSQL's 1.39. Q11's CPU factor is therefore a fix-COUNT factor (F_work 1.496357x, owned by IMP-006) and not a per-fix cost factor. Q11 does not contradict Q08/Q09/Q10, where the unfix/boost path was measured on a different access pattern; it bounds the claim: on a single-threaded index-probe workload with no misses, CUBRID's buffer manager is not the more expensive one. IMP-013's priority should be re-derived from the queries where it IS separable, and Q11 added as a regression control.
q_evidence.Q15: Q15 adds a HIT-path measurement taken while the miss path is simultaneously at its worst, so the two are separable in the same profile. Per logical session CUBRID spends pgbuf_fix_release 1.88% + pgbuf_unfix 0.92% + pgbuf_unlatch_void_zone_bcb 0.92% + __pthread_mutex_lock 1.22% = 4.94% = 1.936 core-s on fix/unfix/latch/LRU surgery, against PostgreSQL's clock-sweep PinBuffer 0.93% + LWLockAttemptLock 0.69% = 1.62% = 0.338 core-s - a 5.7x ratio, on a workload where CUBRID performs FEWER total page fetches than PostgreSQL (1,388,220 against 2,250,257) because its pages are twice the size. Ranked below IMP-002/IMP-007 for Q15 because much of this volume is a consequence of the miss rate those two govern. Raw: profile-cubrid-flat-nocg.txt, profile-pg-flat-nocg.txt, q15-bands.txt. Evidence type: profile attribution.

improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked 2 of 2 new Q08 candidates. It owns the largest profile band on either engine and is the lever that converts CUBRID's 6.6x work advantage into a wall win rather than a 16% CPU margin, but it is not the factor that loses Q08 - F_cpu = 0.838224x already favours CUBRID, and only F_units = 1.373763x is above 1.0, which is IMP-012's. Explanations rejected in favour of this one: 'CUBRID is CPU-hungrier' (rejected by F_cpu = 0.838224x and 0.7391x the instructions) and 'IMP-008's generic DB_VALUE comparator dominates' (rejected by tp_value_compare_with_error 0.59% + eval_value_rel_cmp 0.50% + mr_cmpval_* 1.02% = 2.11%, an order of magnitude below the 27.41% buffer band).

alternative: IMP-010 - same subsystem, but the insertion-position defect for newly READ pages (private vs shared LRU chosen by thread identity). Fixing IMP-010 changes WHERE pages land; fixing IMP-013 changes WHETHER the list is touched at all on a hit.
containment: IMP-002 - that candidate is retention failure at a working set near the pool size and already lists pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb among the symbols in Q04's miss-path profile. IMP-013 is the HIT-path CPU cost of the same bookkeeping, a different quantity: IMP-002 costs physical reads, IMP-013 costs CPU on pages that were found.
IMP-007 - the synchronous single-page pread that serves the misses IMP-002 causes; IMP-013 is the cost of the hits.

improvements.risk: medium-high on performance regression: suppressing or batching boosts changes eviction order, so a workload whose hot set currently survives BECAUSE of aggressive boosting could start missing - and Q08 measures that a miss costs 0.4099 core-s per GiB of re-read. Option (a) is the only variant shippable without a full buffer-pool re-validation.
improvements.root_cause_title: Every page unfix on a HIT path performs mutex-protected LRU doubly-linked-list surgery plus zone rebalancing (pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb), so a plan that touches 6.6x fewer tuples than PostgreSQL's nets only a 16% total-CPU advantage: 27.41% of CUBRID's profile sits in pgbuf fix/unfix/LRU and 5.32% in libpthread, against PostgreSQL's 3.70% clock-sweep pin/unpin with no list and no mutex
improvements.upstream_precedent: No precedent in the pinned CUBRID history for removing or batching the LRU boost. The closest thing is the age-based suppression rule the same function's comment documents at page_buffer.c:10086-10098, which shows the cost was anticipated by the original author for a repeat-fix pattern - and is why option (a) is proposed first.
improvements.validation_criteria: pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb plus libpthread share on Q08 drops below 3% with pgbuf_fix_release unchanged; Q08 total_query_cpu drops by >= 0.3 core-s per statement; Q08 per-statement read-syscall count does NOT increase (the regression that matters - a worse eviction order shows up as more pool churn, which Q08 measures at 0.4099 core-s per GiB); Q01, Q03, Q04 and Q06 walls not regressed, since those are the sequential-scan queries whose retention IMP-002 already flags.

improvements.correctness_risk: None to result correctness: selectivity is a cost input, not a semantic filter, and no operator behaviour changes. Regression risk is plan churn - cardinality estimates rise on every FK-joined query, so hash and merge plans become reachable where NL was previously chosen. The campaign's own Q01-Q22 set is the regression suite; Q08 is the specific counter-case that must not flip.

improvements.denominator: per measured statement of the same query on the same engine, same data, same buffer budget, same parallelism setting; the only difference is the join method on the orders and supplier levels
improvements.difficulty_reason: The structural predicate already exists in-tree and is unit-testable: qo_is_pk_fk_full_join() (src/optimizer/query_graph.c:9955) already walks QO_NODE_INDEXES, tests SM_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGN_KEY and compares fk_info->ref_class_pk_btid against the parent's PK B-tree ID. The work is threading an FK-aware override into planner_visit_node()'s term loop (src/optimizer/query_planner.c:7920-7936) so the covered terms contribute 1/parent_cardinality once, instead of each contributing its own selectivity, plus a guard against applying two FKs to the same term set.
improvements.effect_range: Lower bound 1.5425x on Q09's wall by direct A/B (10.980999 s -> 7.118999 s), i.e. R_wall 2.115055x -> 1.371218x. Not generalisable to a fixed percentage: the effect is whatever the mis-costed plan choice is worth on a given query, zero where the NL choice happens to be correct (Q08 is a measured positive control where forcing the hash shape makes CUBRID 1.5123x SLOWER). Effects must not be summed with IMP-011 or IMP-003, which act on the same plan decision.

improvements.explanation: CUBRID scores the two halves of a composite FK join as independent equalities and multiplies them, collapsing a 3.26 M-row join to an estimated 2 rows; the index-nested-loop chain is then costed as if almost nothing flows through it and wins by 27.3x on the cost scale, while measurement shows it is 1.5425x slower than the hash plan the same executor already runs at 6.23 active units.
improvements.implementation_direction: In planner_visit_node()'s sarged-term loop (src/optimizer/query_planner.c:7920-7936), before multiplying term selectivities, detect the subset of join terms between the two joined node sets that together cover every column of a foreign key whose parent side is the other node's primary key - reusing the existing qo_is_pk_fk_full_join()/QO_INDEX_ENTRY walk from src/optimizer/query_graph.c:9955 rather than adding new catalog access. For that subset contribute a single factor 1/parent_cardinality instead of the per-term product, and mark the terms consumed so a second FK cannot be applied to the same terms (PostgreSQL's costsize.c:5940-5960 guard is the precedent). Leave single-column FK joins on the existing path initially, since the product degenerates to one factor there and the histogram estimate may be better than 1/parent_cardinality.
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: Per join term, qo_equal_selectivity() (src/optimizer/query_planner.c:10189-10238) produces one selectivity for one column pair: histogram_get_join_selectivity() if histograms answer, else 1/MAX(lhs_icard, rhs_icard) from index cardinality, else DEFAULT_EQUIJOIN_SELECTIVITY. planner_visit_node() then multiplies every term's selectivity into a single factor (query_planner.c:7927 'selectivity *= QO_TERM_SELECTIVITY (term);') with only a 1/cardinality floor (:7928), and applies it to the cross-product cardinality (:7936). Nothing in that path knows that two terms can be two halves of one composite key. On Q09 the two halves of fk_lineitem_partsupp are scored 1.00319E-05 (ps_suppkey=l_suppkey, ~1/99,682 supplier NDV) and 5E-07 (p_partkey=l_partkey, 1/2,000,000 part NDV); their product 5.016E-12 applied to 8,015 x 59,986,052 prints 'card 2' where the true value is 3,261,613.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: calc_joinrel_size_estimate() calls get_foreign_key_join_selectivity() BEFORE any clauselist product is formed (src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c:5698). That function iterates root->fkey_list (:5830), and when the join clauses cover all nkeys of an FK it REMOVES them from the restrictlist and substitutes fkselec *= 1.0/ref_tuples (:6008), i.e. the exact 1/8,000,000 that the FK guarantees, with an explicit guard that puts the clauses back if it cannot match all of them (:5940-5960, 'chicken out and ignore this FK; applying its selectivity might result in double-counting'). The in-tree comment at :5810-5813 names this exact failure mode: 'especially for multi-column FKs where that function's assumption that the clauses are independent falls down badly'.

improvements.priority_justification: Largest single factor in Q09's 2.115055x gap: the direct same-engine A/B is 1.542492x, which alone would move R_wall to 1.371218x. Independently confirmed from the PostgreSQL side, where forcing CUBRID's shape costs PostgreSQL 1.384468x. Data-independent defect: any join whose predicate set covers a multi-column FK is mis-estimated by the same NDV-product ratio at any scale.
improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked first among Q09's candidates because it is the only one whose removal is measured to change the wall by more than the block band: 1.5425x by direct A/B against a 3.20% CUBRID band. IMP-013 is second (11.68 core-s/statement, the dominant share of the 1.297496x same-shape CPU residual), IMP-007 third (9.05 core-s/statement kernel read path, itself 23% smaller under the correct plan), IMP-003 fourth (real 34.0x error, shown not to change the plan alone), IMP-005 fifth (no wall effect, evidence-integrity only).

improvements.explanation: CUBRID decides at plan time that the query COULD use hash aggregation, abandons that decision at run time, and then still applies the plan-time flag as a veto on parallelising the sort it actually runs - so the one node that reduces 1,147,084 rows to 381,105 groups is the only serial node in an otherwise 6-worker plan.
improvements.implementation_direction: Replace the plan-time flag with the runtime state at the single decision point. (a) Add the runtime hash state to SORT_LISTFILE_PX_ARG (or pass the AGGREGATE_HASH_CONTEXT) and change external_sort.c:5230-5234 from `if (px == NULL || px->hash_eligible)` to a test that only refuses parallelism while hash aggregation is STILL LIVE - i.e. hash_eligible && state != HS_REJECT_ALL. When the executor has set HS_REJECT_ALL the remaining work is exactly the /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ path, which is already parallel-safe. (b) Independently, give the partial-list sort at query_executor.c:5571-5573 a SORT_LISTFILE_PX_ARG too; today it passes none, so even a fixed (a) leaves that sort serial by construction. (c) Optional follow-up: when HS_REJECT_ALL is set, stop paying for the discarded hash path at all - Q10's profile still spends 1.32% (mht_get_hash_number 0.95 + qexec_hash_gby_agg_tuple 0.37) on hashing whose result is thrown away.

Utilization rises from U = 3.42875 to U = 3.76620 (TWU 3.4245 -> 3.7477, an independent estimate agreeing to 0.49%). Trace node deltas: GROUPBY 3834 ms -> 2565 ms serial-to-parallel (-33.1%); external-sort pages 75,893 -> 24,088 (-68.3%); group-by sort temp ioreads 66,611 -> 0; whole-statement ioreads 76,808 -> 11,646 (-84.8%); the temp list-file re-scan that feeds the sort 805 ms -> 274 ms. The join subtree is unchanged within noise (3168 ms -> 3287 ms), confirming the A/B moved only the aggregation.
mechanism_cubrid: Per group-by execution: qexec_groupby() builds SORT_LISTFILE_PX_ARG gby_px and sets gby_px.hash_eligible = gbstate.hash_eligible (query_executor.c:5657), where gbstate.hash_eligible came from buildlist->g_hash_eligible - a PLAN-TIME boolean set in pt_to_buildlist_proc (xasl_generation.c:16563) purely from the shape of the select list and HAVING clause. sort_listfile() then calls sort_check_parallelism(), whose SORT_GROUP_BY branch begins `if (px == NULL || px->hash_eligible) return 1;` (external_sort.c:5230-5234) and therefore returns a degree of 1 before it ever looks at input_list->page_cnt or asks worker_manager::try_reserve_workers() for threads. For Q10 the executor has, by that point, already given up on hashing: qexec_hash_gby_agg_tuple() set context->state = HS_REJECT_ALL (query_executor.c:4845) and dumped the partial hash table to a list file, which the trace prints as 'hash: partial'. So the flag that vetoes parallelism describes a strategy that is no longer in use. The consequence per row: all 1,147,084 tuples are read back from the temp list file, turned into sort keys by qfile_make_sort_key(), compared by qfile_compare_partial_sort_record() over a 7-column key of which 5 are strings, and merged through 75,893 external-sort pages by ONE thread, while 5 worker threads that the very same query already used for the SCAN sit idle.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: PostgreSQL reached the same strategic conclusion for Q10 - hashing 381,105 groups of ~200 bytes does not fit hash_mem (work_mem 4 MB x hash_mem_multiplier 2 = 8 MB), so the planner costed AGG_SORTED cheaper and the executed plan is GroupAggregate, not HashAggregate - but the sort under it is parallel. gather_grouping_paths() (planner.c:8019) walks rel->partial_pathlist, wraps each partial path in create_sort_path() and then in create_gather_merge_path() (:8083), so per row the work is: each of the 5 units (4 launched workers + participating leader) sorts its own ~229,417-tuple share into its own ~43.6 MB external-merge run, and the leader only runs an n-way binary-heap merge (heap_compare_slots, 1.17% of the profile) plus the final GroupAggregate transition. Nothing in that path is conditioned on whether hashing was considered; enable_hashagg / can_hash affect only which ADDITIONAL paths are added at planner.c:7875. Measured: per-worker Sort 3227->3333 ms i.e. ~106 ms of sort work in parallel, against CUBRID's 3834 ms in one thread.

There is no hashing-related condition anywhere in the function.

improvements.priority_justification: Largest single measured factor in Q10's card: the direct A/B is F_plan = 1.313675x of a 1.689622x total gap, i.e. ln(1.313675)/ln(1.689622) = 52.0% of the whole log-gap, and it is the reason U_C is only 3.42875 against PostgreSQL's 4.63013 on a query where CUBRID is configured for parallelism=6 and actually reaches 6 workers on the driving heap scan.

q_evidence.Q11: Q11 NEGATIVE CONTROL, by executed A/B rather than by argument. Q11's GROUPBY is reported `hash: partial` exactly as Q10's was, so the plan-time hash-eligible flag is set and sort_check_parallelism()'s SORT_GROUP_BY veto (external_sort.c:5228-5234) IS armed. But the controlled block measures /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ at 1.340000 s against native 1.342000 s - F_plan 1.001493x, inside the 1.28% CUBRID block band - and the variant's own trace still shows no `parallel workers` sub-line on GROUPBY. The reason is size: Q11's group-by sorts 323,920 rows through 1,516 sort pages, against Q10's 75,893, so with the veto removed compute_parallel_degree still returns 1. Result rows are identical between native and variant (34,740 extracted rows, same SHA-256). Q11 therefore bounds IMP-015: the veto only costs anything when the fallback sort is large enough to have been parallelised, and Q11 is the regression control that a fix must not change.
q_evidence.Q15: Q15 is the first TRACE-LEVEL proof that the plan-time hash-eligible flag alone serialises the group-by, with no runtime abandonment involved anywhere in the picture - and, unlike Q11, at a size where removing the veto DOES yield parallelism. Native Q15 trace: GROUPBY (time: 2644, hash: partial, sort: true, page: 16266, rows: 100000) and GROUPBY (time: 2636, ...) with NO `parallel workers` sub-line on either, i.e. 5,280 ms of an 11,121 ms statement at one active unit, while the sibling SCAN nodes in the same statement run at `parallel workers: 6`. With /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ - which clears buildlist->g_hash_eligible at xasl_generation.c:16556-16559, the exact flag sort_check_parallelism() tests at external_sort.c:5229-5234 - the same nodes report `hash: false, sort: true` plus `(parallel workers: 3, time: 330..338)` and drop to 2305/2220 ms, with the statement total falling 11,121 -> 10,305 ms. Whole-session effect is stated as a BOUND, not a direct A/B, because the variant's gated block was REJECTED by the section 12 WARM gate on all four attempts (trailing spread 3.94%, 5.37%, 6.16%, 5.68%, all above the 3.00% sanity bound): across 80 uncounted variant sessions the median is 9.2615 s against a 60-session native median of 10.4565 s (-11.33%), and 79 of the 80 variant sessions are faster than the FASTEST of the 60 native sessions (native min 10.334 s; variant max 9.818 s excluding one 11.111 s outlier). The instability is itself part of the finding. Q15 also rules IMP-016/IMP-017 OUT as the cause here: group/tuple selectivity is 100,000/2,265,714 = 0.0441, nowhere near the 0.5f heuristic, and the trace shows hash aggregation is USED (hash: partial), not abandoned. Raw: q15-trace-cubrid.out, variants/q15-trace-cubrid-nohashagg.out, Q15-cubrid-nohashagg-warm-attempt{1,2,3,4}.json, Q15-cubrid-warm-block{1,2,3}.json. Evidence type: lower bound.
q_evidence.Q18: Q18 BOUNDARY CASE and the campaign's largest measured serial share for this defect -- but NOT a direct A/B, and the report says so explicitly. ARMED: Q18's subquery `select l_orderkey from lineitem group by l_orderkey having sum(l_quantity) > 300` is marked g_hash_eligible at XASL generation (xasl_generation.c:16556-16568) purely because sum() is hash-aggregatable; at runtime the 2 MB max_agg_hash_size cannot hold the 15,000,000 groups that independent ground truth confirms (q18-groundtruth-*.out subquery_groups_prehaving=15000000), so the executor degrades to sorting -- q18-trace-cubrid.out reports `GROUPBY (time: 29563, hash: partial, sort: true, page: 422017, ioread: 459086, rows: 624)`, i.e. the veto condition is exactly the IMP-015 condition. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: 89.10 s of the 140.50 s four-statement block runs at ~1 active unit (63.4%, time-weighted over 1,253 real sampling intervals, Q18-cubrid-headline-telemetry-intervals.json) against 44.11 s (31.4%) at ~6 units; the per-statement shape repeats four times as ~11 s of 6-unit parallel heap scan followed by ~22 s of 1-unit group-by. The profile attributes that phase to CUBRID's single `transaction` comm (18.36 of 77.55 resolved points), led by qfile_compare_partial_sort_record 3.27% and sort_run_merge 0.80%. WHY NO DIRECT A/B ON Q18: the /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ lever that isolated this on Q10 does NOT isolate it here, because on Q18 the partial hash pass is doing real work (reducing 59,986,052 rows toward 15,000,000 groups) rather than merely being abandoned. Removing hash eligibility removed that work too: the measured block went 37.452998 s -> 40.173998 s (+7.3% SLOWER, Q18-cubrid-nohashagg-headline.json), TWU FELL 2.7041 -> 1.8912, serial tail ROSE 12.548 s -> 30.578 s, and the trace went `hash: partial, time: 29563` -> `hash: false, time: 43073` (q18-trace-nohashagg.out). The sort did not become parallel. Q18 therefore contributes an UPPER BOUND, not a factor: perfectly parallelising the 22.28 s/statement serial phase to the 6 units the scan already reaches would give at most 37.45 s -> ~18.9 s (~1.98x), ignoring merge/gather overhead.
q_evidence.Q18_alternative_rejection: Q18 MEASURES the rejection of this entry's own recorded alternative ('stop marking the query hash-eligible when the optimizer's group-count estimate cannot fit max_agg_hash_size'). /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ is exactly that alternative applied by hand, and on Q18 it is a 7.3% REGRESSION (37.452998 s -> 40.173998 s) because it also discards the partial hash pre-aggregation. This upgrades the alternative's status from argued-rejection to measured-rejection and confirms the primary implementation_direction: the fix must keep hash pre-aggregation AND parallelise the fallback sort, i.e. decide parallelism from the RUNTIME hash state, never by suppressing hash-eligibility at plan time.

improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked 1 of 3 new Q10 candidates. It owns the single largest measured factor (1.313675x direct A/B = 52.0% of the log-gap), it is the cheapest change (one condition), and its correctness surface is already covered by an executed A/B that returned the identical result. IMP-016 is ranked 2: it is the upstream trigger and a fix there would also recover Q10, but it changes an estimation heuristic used by every hash-aggregate query, so its blast radius is far larger for the same measured Q10 gain. IMP-017 is ranked 3: it is a real defect and a 3-line fix, but on its own it changes no Q10 number (the 512M probe moved GROUPBY 3834 -> 3761 ms and page 75,893 -> 73,606, inside the 1.22% CUBRID block spread), because HS_REJECT_ALL is set by the selectivity test and not by the memory limit. Explanations considered and REJECTED for Q10's gap: (i) 'CUBRID chose the wrong join shape' - rejected by the CUBRID-side USE_HASH(lineitem, customer) variant measuring 13.809/13.869 s, 1.94x SLOWER than native, and by the PostgreSQL-side A/B showing CUBRID's shape is the faster one on PostgreSQL too (2.484 s vs 4.219 s); (ii) 'the working set does not fit CUBRID's 8 GiB buffer' (IMP-002) - rejected by /proc/<cub_server>/io read_bytes delta = 0 and device read delta 0.02 MiB across the whole diagnostic block, i.e. zero physical reads; (iii) 'the 2 MB aggregate hash budget is the trigger' - rejected by source: the `while (context->hash_size > mem_limit)` loop at query_executor.c:4808-4835 only EVICTS and never assigns HS_REJECT_ALL, which has exactly one assignment site (:4845, the selectivity test).

alternative: Stop marking the query hash-eligible when the optimizer's own group-count estimate cannot fit max_agg_hash_size, so hash_eligible is false from the start and the existing veto is never armed. Rejected as the primary direction for Q10: the optimizer's group estimate here is 237,795 against a true 381,105 (0.62x) and the decision would rest on that estimate, whereas the fix above rests on the runtime state the executor has already computed. Recorded as the cheaper mitigation if IMP-016 is fixed first.
Expose /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ as guidance. Rejected: a hint is not a fix, and the query is canonical TPC-H text that must not be modified (SSOT section 6).
containment: IMP-016 - the reason this veto is armed on Q10 at all. IMP-016 is why the executor reached HS_REJECT_ALL; IMP-015 is why reaching it costs the query its parallelism. They are independent: fixing IMP-016 alone would make Q10 hash-aggregate (and the veto would then be correct), fixing IMP-015 alone recovers the measured 1.313675x without touching the estimator. Ranked 1 of 3 because it is the localized change.
IMP-017 - the same 2 MB budget, but the defect that the budget cannot be changed at all. IMP-017 is why the memory-limit explanation could not be tested by experiment on this server process.

IMP-012 - also a parallel-degree defect, but at compute_parallel_degree()'s SCAN branch. Q10's driving heap scan DOES reach 6 workers ('parallel workers: 6, readrows: 2380011..2525461'), so IMP-012's saturation is not what limits Q10; the group-by veto is. Q10 is recorded on IMP-012 as a negative control.

Does NOT fire on Q16: the trace shows 'GROUPBY ... (parallel workers: 3)' in both the native and the NO_PARALLEL_SCAN run, i.e. sort_check_parallelism() admitted the sort. Q16's serial phase belongs to the post-sort finalize loop (IMP-023), which is a different code path.

improvements.risk: low: one condition and one missing argument. Requires a plan-stability and input-order-sensitivity suite because it changes how many threads a group-by sort takes from the shared worker pool.
improvements.root_cause_title: sort_check_parallelism() unconditionally refuses parallelism for a SORT_GROUP_BY whenever the query was marked hash-aggregate-eligible, even after the executor has already ABANDONED hash aggregation at runtime (HS_REJECT_ALL), so the entire sort-based fallback group-by runs single-threaded while every other node of the same plan runs at 5-6 workers - 3834 ms of Q10's 8048 ms traced execution at one active unit, and a 1.313675x direct same-engine A/B
improvements.upstream_precedent: Partial precedent inside the pinned source itself: the ANALYTIC caller of the same machinery already refuses to apply this veto - query_executor.c:21886 sets `anl_px.hash_eligible = 0; /* GROUP_BY only; never skip ANALYTIC parallelism on this account */`. So the codebase already contains the judgement that hash eligibility is not a reason to serialise a sort; the GROUP_BY path simply never had that judgement applied to the post-abandonment case. No CBRD issue/PR in the pinned history (607f1ee9, incl. PR #7441) changes sort_check_parallelism's SORT_GROUP_BY branch.
improvements.validation_criteria: 1) Q10 CUBRID trace shows `GROUPBY (... hash: partial ...)` WITH a '(parallel workers: N>=2)' sub-line and group-by sort ioread ~0, and the 20-row result is byte-identical to raw/Q10/q10-correctness-cubrid.out under the section-11 comparator. 2) Q10 median wall <= 5.70 s (the measured 5.426 s controlled block plus the 1.22% CUBRID block spread and a margin), U >= 3.70. 3) An input-order-sensitive aggregate suite (GROUP_CONCAT, and MIN/MAX with agg_hash_respect_order=y) returns the serial result. 4) Q01/Q03/Q05 group-by wall not regressed and their plan shapes unchanged. 5) worker-pool pressure: with parallelism=6 the group-by sort must not reserve workers a concurrently running SCAN needs - measure Q01-Q22 stream wall, not just Q10.

Making group_count honest across eviction is a localized counter fix in the eviction loop (query_executor.c:4808-4835, symmetrical with the hash_size bookkeeping two lines above). Deciding what the abandonment rule SHOULD be is an estimation change with campaign-wide blast radius, and a hardcoded 0.5f is not obviously replaceable by another constant.
improvements.effect_range: On Q10 the whole observable effect is the fallback IMP-015 prices at 1.313675x; fixing IMP-016 alone would let Q10 hash-aggregate and is expected to be at least as good, but HOW good is NOT measured here and is deliberately not claimed, because the server-parameter experiment that would show it is blocked by IMP-017. Independently recoverable and measured: the 1.32% of profile spent on the discarded hash table. Lower bound on the class of affected queries: any GROUP BY whose groups do not fit 2 MB and whose rows-per-group is below ~3, i.e. most TPC-H customer/part-grained aggregations.
improvements.evidence_event: The runtime hash state printed by CUBRID's own trace, against the true selectivity measured on the same data by both engines. NATIVE trace: `GROUPBY (time: 3834, hash: partial, ...)`; query_dump.c:3948-3951 maps 'hash: partial' to HS_REJECT_ALL, and HS_REJECT_ALL has exactly ONE assignment site in the tree (query_executor.c:4845), so the 0.5f test provably fired. True selectivity from ground-truth counts both engines answer identically: 381,105 groups / 1,147,084 tuples = 0.332243. Selectivity of every orderkey-ordered input prefix, measured on both engines (q10-selectivity-probe-*.out): first 2,001 tuples 850/2001 = 0.424788; 5,000 -> 2133/5000 = 0.426600; 20,000 -> 8444/20000 = 0.422200; 200,000 -> 81617/200000 = 0.408085. Every one of them is below 0.5, so an honest group counter could not have tripped the test.
improvements.evidence_type: direct A/B for the 'hash: partial' state and for the true selectivity (both engines agree on every ground-truth count); upper bound for the counter overstatement (>= 1.1771x); profile attribution for the 1.32% discarded-hash band
improvements.explanation: The heuristic asks 'are almost all rows their own group, so is hashing pointless?', but it asks a counter that the eviction path inflates, and the eviction path is guaranteed to run because the budget is 2 MB and the query has 381,105 wide groups - so a query with 3.01 rows per group is classified as very-high-selectivity and loses hashing.
improvements.implementation_direction: (a) Make the counter honest: decrement context->group_count in the eviction loop at query_executor.c:4830-4834, symmetrically with hash_size, or keep a separate `groups_ever_seen` for statistics and use mht_count(hash_table) for the ratio. This is a strict improvement regardless of what the threshold becomes. (b) Reconsider the abandonment rule. The condition it is trying to detect - 'hashing buys nothing because nearly every row is its own group' - is a memory/benefit question, which is what PostgreSQL's hash_agg_check_limits() actually measures. The minimal version keeps the 0.5f test but evaluates it on the honest ratio and re-evaluates it instead of latching, so a statement that starts dense-looking can recover. (c) Longer term, prefer spilling over abandoning: the partial list file that qdata_save_agg_hentry_to_list already writes is most of a spill mechanism; making it a hash-partitioned spill that keeps resident groups aggregating would remove the flip entirely and would also remove IMP-015's trigger.
improvements.measurement: Gap between the counter the code uses and the quantity it claims to measure: the test must have seen group_count/tuple_count > 0.5 while the true ratio never exceeds 0.424788 on any measured prefix and is 0.332243 globally - a minimum overstatement of 1.1771x (0.5/0.424788) and 1.5049x against the global value. Independently, the shape that forces eviction is measured: 381,105 groups, group key = 7 columns of which 5 are strings (c_name 25, c_phone 15, n_name 25, c_address 40, c_comment 117 bytes wide), plus the full first tuple stored per group, against mem_limit = 2 MB. The A/B cost of the resulting fallback is the 1.313675x recorded on IMP-015. Wasted hash work still paid on the abandoned path: 1.32% of the CUBRID profile (mht_get_hash_number 0.95%, qexec_hash_gby_agg_tuple 0.37%).
mechanism_cubrid: Per row, qexec_hash_gby_agg_tuple() builds the group key, probes the hash table, and on a miss inserts a new entry AND increments context->group_count (:4740-4741); on a hit it increments only tuple_count. It then runs `while (context->hash_size > mem_limit)` (:4808), and for each iteration writes the least-recently-used entry to the partial list file, writes its first tuple to the group-by list file, subtracts the entry's key and value sizes from hash_size and calls mht_rem - but leaves group_count untouched (:4830-4834). Finally, once tuple_count passes 2000, it computes group_count/tuple_count and, above 0.5f, sets state = HS_REJECT_ALL permanently (:4838-4849). So each of the 381,105 groups can be counted more than once - once per (eviction, re-encounter) cycle - and the ratio is a monotonically drifting overestimate of selectivity rather than a measurement of it. For Q10 the drift is guaranteed: a group's value holds the whole ~200-byte output tuple plus a 5-string key, so at most a few thousand of 381,105 groups are ever resident.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: PostgreSQL never has this counter. The hashed-vs-sorted choice is made ONCE by the planner as a cost comparison (planner.c:7875 add_paths_to_grouping_rel adds an AGG_HASHED path priced by cost_agg with estimate_num_groups(); Q10's 591,526-group estimate against an 8 MB hash_mem made AGG_SORTED cheaper, which is why the executed plan is GroupAggregate). At run time, nodeAgg.c:1866 hash_agg_check_limits() compares REAL allocated bytes and a real group count against hash_mem_limit / hash_ngroups_limit, and on breach calls hash_agg_enter_spill_mode() (:1907), after which lookup_hash_entries() passes p_isnew = NULL so existing groups keep aggregating in memory while only would-be-new groups are written to hash-partitioned tapes (:3029 hashagg_spill_tuple) and reprocessed batch by batch (:2734 agg_refill_hash_table). The strategy never flips, and no counter is left inconsistent.
postgresql_source: src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c:7875 `if (can_hash && cheapest_partial_path != NULL)` and the surrounding add_paths_to_grouping_rel body - PostgreSQL's hashed-vs-sorted decision is a COST comparison between add_path()ed AGG_HASHED and AGG_SORTED paths using estimate_num_groups()/cost_agg, taken once by the planner, not a runtime sample of the first 2000 tuples

src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:1866 hash_agg_check_limits() - the runtime check that corresponds to CUBRID's; note what it tests: actual MemoryContextMemAllocated of the meta/tuples/tval contexts against hash_mem_limit, and hash_ngroups_current against hash_ngroups_limit. There is no selectivity term at all.

src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:1907 hash_agg_enter_spill_mode() and :3029 hashagg_spill_tuple() - when the budget IS exceeded PostgreSQL keeps the groups it already has in the hash table and spills only the tuples that would create NEW groups, into hash-partitioned tapes it later reprocesses (:2734 agg_refill_hash_table). It never discards the hash table and never switches the statement to sorting.
src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:1897-1899 the only 'give up' behaviour in the file is `if (aggstate->hash_ngroups_current > 0 && ...)` guarding progress, i.e. spill is always preferred to abandonment

src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:3086 hash_choose_num_partitions() - the spill fan-out is derived from the estimated input cardinality and hash_mem, so exceeding the budget degrades gracefully with partition count instead of flipping strategy
improvements.priority_justification: It is the trigger that arms IMP-015 on Q10, so it shares the same 1.313675x of a 1.689622x gap, but it is ranked below IMP-015 because the measured recovery is obtained by fixing IMP-015 alone and this change touches an estimator every hash-aggregate query uses. Its own direct cost is additionally the 1.32% of profile (mht_get_hash_number 0.95 + qexec_hash_gby_agg_tuple 0.37) spent building a hash table that is then discarded.

q_evidence.Q11: Q11 NEGATIVE CONTROL, and the most informative one this candidate has. Q11's GROUPBY is also reported `hash: partial`, i.e. HS_REJECT_ALL also fired here - but on Q11 the decision is CORRECT. Measured true group/tuple selectivity, identical on both engines (q11-selectivity.txt): 1.000000 on the first 2,000 tuples (the first prefix at which HASH_AGGREGATE_VH_SELECTIVITY_TUPLE_THRESHOLD=2000 lets the test fire), 1.000000 at 5,040, 1.000000 at 20,000, 0.968610 at 200,000 and 0.940893 over the whole 323,920-tuple input, against 304,774 distinct ps_partkey. Every value is far above the 0.5f threshold, so no drift in `group_count` is needed to explain the abort and none can be inferred. That matters for IMP-016's framing: the 0.5f test is not wrong as a rule, and the candidate's claim must stay narrowly on the undecremented `group_count` (query_executor.c:4740-4741 vs the eviction loop at :4808-4835), which Q10 measures and Q11 cannot. Q11 is the control that a fix must not flip: after any change, Q11 must still choose the sort.
q_evidence.Q18: Q18 supplies the group-count scale at which the 2 MB budget collapses: the subquery forms 15,000,000 groups (independent ground truth, both engines) from 59,986,052 rows, and the executor reports `hash: partial` with 422,017 temp pages and 459,086 ioreads spilled (q18-trace-cubrid.out). PostgreSQL meets the same situation by PLANNING a partitioned spill -- `Partial HashAggregate ... Planned Partitions: 16` in q18-plan-act-pg-noidx.out -- rather than collapsing to a global sort at runtime.

improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked 2 of 3 new Q10 candidates - see IMP-015's ranking_rationale for the full comparison and for the three explanations that were considered and rejected with the numbers that rejected them. Ranked above IMP-017 because it is causally responsible for a measured 1.313675x, whereas IMP-017 changes no Q10 number on its own. Ranked below IMP-015 because the same 1.313675x is recovered by IMP-015's one-condition change, while this candidate's (b)/(c) parts alter strategy selection for every hash-aggregate query in the product.

alternative: Raise max_agg_hash_size so eviction never happens and the counter never drifts. Rejected as a fix: it is blocked outright by IMP-017 (the value is captured in a function-local static), it only moves the threshold for one data size, and it leaves the counter wrong for any workload that does exceed the new budget.

Delete the very-high-selectivity abort entirely and always hash when eligible. Rejected: the heuristic protects the genuinely-almost-unique-key case, where hashing pays a per-row insert plus eviction write for no reduction; Q10 provides no evidence about that case, so removing the guard is unjustified by this measurement.
containment: IMP-015 - the consumer of this defect's output. IMP-016 puts the executor into HS_REJECT_ALL; IMP-015 turns that state into a lost 5-way parallel sort. Fixing either recovers Q10's 1.313675x; fixing IMP-015 is the measured route.
IMP-017 - the reason the memory-limit branch of this root cause could not be tested by experiment: max_agg_hash_size cannot be changed on a running server.

IMP-001 - also an aggregation-path candidate, but about the per-row NUMERIC accumulator inside qdata_evaluate_aggregate_list, not about which aggregation strategy is chosen. Both are visible in Q10's profile (numeric compare/read 0.76+0.56%) and they do not overlap.

improvements.risk: medium: (a) is a counter fix, but (b)/(c) change which aggregation strategy real queries take, and therefore group output order and worker-pool pressure. Needs the full Q01-Q22 plan-and-order diff, not just Q10.
improvements.root_cause_title: Hash aggregation is abandoned for the whole statement by a hardcoded 0.5f very-high-selectivity heuristic that is evaluated on a group counter which the LRU eviction path never decrements, so the 2 MB max_agg_hash_size budget makes the estimate drift upward until it crosses 0.5 on a query whose true group/tuple selectivity is 0.332243 and whose every measured input prefix is at most 0.424788
improvements.upstream_precedent: No CBRD issue/PR in the pinned history (607f1ee9, including PR #7441) touches HASH_AGGREGATE_VH_SELECTIVITY_THRESHOLD or the group_count bookkeeping. The closest in-tree precedent for the direction is CUBRID's own hash-JOIN path, which already degrades by spilling rather than by abandoning the strategy (query_hash_scan.h:128 hash_list_scan_type IN_MEM / HYBRID / HASH_FILE), i.e. the codebase already implements 'spill, do not flip' for the join side of the same problem.
improvements.validation_criteria: 1) With (a) applied, Q10's trace shows the honest ratio path: either 'hash: true' (hashing retained) or 'hash: partial' with a documented reason, and the 20-row result stays byte-identical to raw/Q10/q10-correctness-cubrid.out. 2) A synthetic matrix over rows-per-group in {1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 10.0} x group-set-size in {fits 2 MB, 10x, 100x} shows the abandonment decision depends on rows-per-group and NOT on whether eviction occurred. 3) No Q01-Q22 group-by output-order change for queries with an ORDER BY, and an explicit order check for those without. 4) Q01 (4 groups, fits trivially) and Q05/Q07 (small group sets) unchanged in plan, wall and hash state.

improvements.correctness_risk: None to query results: mem_limit only bounds when entries are written to the partial list file, and both the resident and the evicted path already produce the same groups (the whole spill path is exercised by Q10 today). The behavioural change is that max_agg_hash_size starts working, so a site that had unknowingly been running at the 2 MB default will begin honouring a larger configured value and use more server memory.

src/query/query_executor.c:4808 `while (context->hash_size > (int) mem_limit)` - the only consumer; note also the UINT64 -> int narrowing cast in the comparison
