improvements.denominator: one traced statement per configuration on the same server process, same WARM state, same plan (cost 649494), same 1,147,084 input tuples and 381,105 output groups
improvements.difficulty_reason: Delete one storage-class keyword, or hoist the read to the per-statement setup that already exists (qexec_alloc_agg_hash_context). The value is used only as a comparison bound in one loop; prm_get_bigint_value is already called per statement elsewhere in the same file, so there is no measured reason to cache it per process.
improvements.effect_range: Zero measured effect on Q10's wall by itself, because HS_REJECT_ALL on Q10 is set by the selectivity test and not by the memory limit (query_executor.c:4845 is the only assignment site; the eviction loop only evicts). Its value is that it restores a control: with the parameter live, the memory-limit component of IMP-016 becomes testable, and operators regain the documented ability to trade memory for aggregate spill. No performance claim is made.
improvements.evidence_event: A 256x parameter change with no observable effect. Probe (q10-bigagghash-trace.out): `SET SYSTEM PARAMETERS 'max_agg_hash_size=512M'; SET TRACE ON; <Q10>; SHOW TRACE;` in one gated csql session on the campaign server. Result: still `GROUPBY (time: 3761, hash: partial, sort: true, page: 73606, ioread: 58563, rows: 381105)` - same 'hash: partial' abandonment, same order of sort spill - against the unmodified `GROUPBY (time: 3834, hash: partial, sort: true, page: 75893, ioread: 66611, rows: 381105)`. A 512 MB budget would have held all 381,105 groups (~76 MB of key+tuple) with no eviction at all.
improvements.evidence_type: direct A/B (the null result is the evidence: a 256x parameter change produced deltas inside the block-noise band) plus source reading for the mechanism
improvements.explanation: The per-row hash-aggregate path caches the aggregate memory budget in a function-local static, so the first hash-aggregate query executed after a server start fixes that budget for every query the process will ever run.
improvements.implementation_direction: Drop `static` at query_executor.c:4643 - prm_get_bigint_value is a cheap array read and this path already does far more work per row - or, preferred, read the budget once per statement in qexec_alloc_agg_hash_context() (:27694) and store it in AGGREGATE_HASH_CONTEXT next to hash_size, so the per-row loop compares against a field instead of calling into the parameter subsystem. Fix the UINT64 -> int narrowing in the same edit by making hash_size/mem_limit the same unsigned 64-bit type.
improvements.measurement: GROUPBY node time 3834 ms -> 3761 ms (-1.90%) and external-sort pages 75,893 -> 73,606 (-3.01%) for a 256x increase in the nominal budget; both deltas are inside the measured 1.22% CUBRID block-median spread and the trace's own run-to-run variation, and the abandonment verdict is bit-identical. Whole-statement SELECT time 8048 ms -> 8030 ms (-0.22%). Expected effect had the parameter taken hold: no eviction at all, i.e. hash_size never exceeds mem_limit and the eviction loop at :4808 never executes.
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: Per row on the hash-aggregate path, qexec_hash_gby_agg_tuple() executes `static UINT64 mem_limit = prm_get_bigint_value (PRM_ID_MAX_AGG_HASH_SIZE);` (query_executor.c:4643). C++ function-local statics with dynamic initializers are initialized on FIRST execution and never re-evaluated; every subsequent call - including calls from other sessions, other transactions and other queries, since cub_server is one multi-threaded process - reuses the cached value. The only consumer is the eviction bound at :4808. Therefore changing max_agg_hash_size through SET SYSTEM PARAMETERS, or through any per-session mechanism, cannot change the eviction behaviour of a server that has already run one hash-aggregate statement. There is also a UINT64 -> int narrowing cast in the comparison, so a budget above INT_MAX would compare against a truncated bound.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: PostgreSQL computes the equivalent budget per executor state, not per process: ExecInitAgg calls hash_agg_set_limits(hashentrysize, totalGroups, 0, &aggstate->hash_mem_limit, &aggstate->hash_ngroups_limit, &aggstate->hash_planned_partitions) (nodeAgg.c:4396) from the live work_mem and hash_mem_multiplier, hash_agg_check_limits() then reads aggstate->hash_mem_limit on every group insert (:1871), and agg_refill_hash_table() recomputes the limits again for each spill batch (:2831). A session-level `SET work_mem` therefore takes effect on the next statement, which is exactly the behaviour CUBRID's parameter documentation implies but does not deliver.

src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:4396 (ExecInitAgg) hash_agg_set_limits(...) - the limits are computed per AggState at executor init from the live work_mem / hash_mem_multiplier, so a SET in the session takes effect on the next statement
src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:2831-2834 (agg_refill_hash_table) hash_agg_set_limits() is called AGAIN per spill batch, i.e. PostgreSQL re-reads the budget even within one statement
src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c:3141-3147 hash_create_memory() derives maxBlockSize from the live work_mem for the same reason
improvements.priority_justification: It changes no Q10 headline number by itself - the 256x parameter change moved GROUPBY from 3834 ms to 3761 ms and sort pages from 75,893 to 73,606, inside the 1.22% CUBRID block spread - so it is not on the critical path of the 1.689622x gap. It is P2 rather than P3 because it silently disables the only operator-facing control over the aggregate hash budget, which is what made the memory-limit hypothesis for IMP-016 untestable without a server restart.

q_evidence.Q18: Q18 independently reconfirms that max_agg_hash_size cannot be changed at session level on this build: `SET SYSTEM PARAMETERS 'max_agg_hash_size=256M'` returns `ERROR: Cannot change system parameter`, so the frozen function-local static this entry describes cannot even be probed from a session. Q18 therefore measures the SESSION-SETTABLE half of the same aggregation memory budget: sort_buffer_size 2M -> 256M cuts the subquery GROUPBY spill from 422,040 to 145,717 temp pages (-65.5%) and ioread from 455,485 to 225,405 (-50.5%), shortening the traced statement 41.106 s -> 38.257 s (-6.93%) and the GROUPBY node 29,230 ms -> 26,400 ms (-9.68%). Cleanly controlled: the parallel scan phase is unchanged across the pair (11,836 ms vs 11,813 ms) and the -2.849 s statement delta is accounted for by the -2.830 s GROUPBY delta. Evidence type: direct A/B (same engine, controlled parameter). Artifacts raw/Q18/q18-sortbuf-{2M,256M}-trace.out.

improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked 3 of 3 new Q10 candidates. It is the only one of the three that changes no Q10 number on its own - the 256x probe moved GROUPBY 3834 -> 3761 ms and sort pages 75,893 -> 73,606, both inside the 1.22% CUBRID block spread - so it cannot compete with IMP-015's 1.313675x direct A/B or with IMP-016's causal ownership of the trigger. It is nonetheless recorded rather than dropped because it is a 1-line defect that silently disables an operator control, and because it is the specific reason this report cannot quantify the memory-limit branch of IMP-016 without a server restart. See IMP-015's ranking_rationale for the rejected whole-query explanations.

alternative: Document max_agg_hash_size as server-start-only. Rejected: the parameter is declared as a normal changeable server parameter and paramdump reports it per server; freezing it at the first query of the process is not a documentable contract, it is a bug, and it silently varies with which query happened to run first after a restart.
containment: IMP-016 - the same 2 MB budget. IMP-016 is about what the budget's eviction does to the selectivity counter; IMP-017 is about the budget being unchangeable. IMP-017 is what made IMP-016's memory-limit hypothesis untestable on this server process without a restart, which the campaign's WARM-state contract (SSOT section 12) makes expensive.
IMP-015 - unrelated mechanically (parallelism veto), but the same statement and the same 1.313675x A/B; ranked above this candidate.

improvements.risk: low: one storage-class/field change. The behavioural risk is that a previously ignored configuration value starts being honoured, so release notes must call it out and a memory high-water-mark test at the default must be part of the change.
improvements.root_cause_title: max_agg_hash_size is read into a FUNCTION-LOCAL STATIC in the per-row hash-aggregate path, so the parameter is frozen at the first hash-aggregate tuple of the server process and can never be changed for the life of that process - a session-level SET SYSTEM PARAMETERS to 512M provably changed nothing
improvements.upstream_precedent: Direct in-tree precedent for the pattern being wrong: the same file reads other parameters per statement rather than caching them in function-local statics (e.g. prm_get_bool_value (PRM_ID_AGG_HASH_RESPECT_ORDER) at query_executor.c:5468, evaluated inside qexec_groupby on every execution). No CBRD issue/PR in the pinned history (607f1ee9, incl. PR #7441) touches query_executor.c:4643.
improvements.validation_criteria: 1) On one server process, `SET SYSTEM PARAMETERS 'max_agg_hash_size=512M'` followed by Q10 with SET TRACE ON must show the eviction loop no longer running - group-by sort page count at or below the 24,088 measured on the /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ variant, or 'hash: true' - and the 20-row result byte-identical to raw/Q10/q10-correctness-cubrid.out. 2) The reverse direction also takes effect: setting 2M back must restore the 75,893-page behaviour in the same session. 3) A budget above INT_MAX must not truncate: set 4G and assert no eviction on a 3 GB group set. 4) Q01-Q22 memory high-water mark measured at the default 2M is unchanged, proving the default path is untouched.

improvements.correctness_risk: None on results: buffer placement and victim order cannot change a query's answer, and Q11's saturated and unsaturated states already return byte-identical rows (the 34,740 extracted result rows of block1 and block3 hash the same, and match PostgreSQL's). The real risk is a PERFORMANCE regression in the workload the private lists were added for: a larger private quota per session means many concurrent sessions can collectively over-commit the pool and evict each other, which is exactly what the ratio-based adaptive quota exists to prevent. Any change must therefore keep the ADAPTIVE term and only raise the CEILING, and must be validated with a many-session workload, not just with this campaign's single-session regime.

improvements.denominator: reads per statement, against a working set of 93,281 partsupp heap pages + 4,057 supplier + index pages = ~97,400 pages of 16 KiB in a 524,288-page (8192 MB) pool, i.e. 18.6% of the pool; and against the measured retention window of ~5,000 pages = 0.95% of the pool
improvements.difficulty_reason: The primary change is one constant and one clamp: PGBUF_PRIVATE_LRU_MAX_HARD_QUOTA (page_buffer.c:1024) and the MIN(...) that applies it (page_buffer.c:14379) already exist, and the quota field they write is already respected by every consumer (PGBUF_LRU_LIST_IS_OVER_QUOTA and the victim paths). Making the cap scale with pgbuf_Pool.num_buffers is a localized arithmetic change with no new mechanism, no new data structure and no plan or semantic effect. It rises to medium if the accompanying MIN_PRIVATE_RATIO floor (page_buffer.c:14193) must also be revisited, which the Q11 measurement cannot separate from the hard cap on this pool size.
improvements.effect_range: Direct A/B on the wall: CUBRID Q11 block median 3.544000 s -> 1.342000 s = 2.6408x, with the plan, the query text, every parameter and the page-fix count constant. The attribution is the trace's own fetch_time, 2,061 ms -> 326 ms of a 3,360 ms -> 1,532 ms statement, i.e. 1,735 ms of the 1,828 ms recovered (94.9%). Total query CPU per statement falls from 3.183 core-s (block1 regime, U=1.00968 x 3.263 s telemetry pair) to 1.355 core-s. This is a LOWER bound on the campaign-wide effect, not an upper bound: Q11 recovers all of it because its working set fits the pool 5.4x over, and a query whose set does not fit would keep a residual. It is also the amount by which every earlier Q11 measurement in this session was wrong, which is why the headline is taken in the saturated state.
improvements.evidence_event: physical data-page reads per statement for an unchanged plan on an unchanged pool, measured three independent ways: CUBRID trace `ioread` per statement (566,103 -> 67,605 -> 0), /proc/<cub_server>/io syscr delta per statement (551,116 -> 253,684 -> 207,599 -> 112 -> 96) and /proc/<cub_server>/io rchar delta per statement (8.406 GiB -> 4.153 GiB -> 3.166 GiB -> ~0, all at 16,384 bytes per read syscall). Device read_bytes delta is 0 throughout, so every one of these reads is an OS page-cache copy, not a disk read.
improvements.implementation_direction: Ordered cheapest first. (1) Scale the cap: replace the constant 5000 at page_buffer.c:1024 with a fraction of pgbuf_Pool.num_buffers (the MIN at page_buffer.c:14380 already bounds it at num_buffers/2, which is the safety this change relies on), so an 8 GB pool does not hand a single session 78 MiB. (2) Revisit the MIN_PRIVATE_RATIO floor at page_buffer.c:14193 in the same change: on this pool the 0.01 floor produces 5,242, so fixing only the constant would move the ceiling by 4% and the measurement would not improve - the two must be changed together, and Q11 is the test that shows it, because it cannot separate them. (3) Make the private->shared escape reachable for a scan pattern: pgbuf_should_move_private_to_shared (page_buffer.c:6951-6984) currently requires 64 fixes while resident; promote a page that survives N over-quota victim passes, or demote instead of victimizing when a private list is over quota, so an over-quota private page lands in the shared pool rather than being recycled. (4) Rejected as the primary direction: exposing num_private_chains as a dynamic parameter. It would let an operator disable the private lists entirely (num_private_LRU_list = 0 turns PGBUF_PAGE_QUOTA_IS_ENABLED off), but it is a workaround for a default that is wrong, and it discards the private lists' intended benefit for many-session OLTP instead of sizing them.
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: Q11's plan is nation sscan -> supplier iscan(fk_supplier_nation) -> partsupp iscan(fk_partsupp_supplier), run twice (main query plus uncorrelated subquery). Each run performs 4,049 index descents and 323,920 heap row lookups scattered over partsupp's 93,281 heap pages. Every page the lookups physically read is unfixed through pgbuf_unlatch_void_zone_bcb (page_buffer.c:6902-6912) onto the TOP of the session's private LRU list, because the query runs on the client transaction thread and therefore has thread_private_lru_index != -1. pgbuf_adjust_quotas sets that list's quota to MIN(activity_share * all_private_quota, PGBUF_PRIVATE_LRU_MAX_HARD_QUOTA=5000, num_buffers/2) at page_buffer.c:14378-14380; with one active session the first term is 0.01*524,288 = 5,242 and the cap is 5,000, so the list holds ~5,000 of the ~97,000 pages the query needs. Beyond quota the list's bottom becomes victim candidates (pgbuf_lru_add_victim_candidate, gated on PGBUF_LRU_LIST_IS_OVER_QUOTA) and pages are recycled. pgbuf_should_move_private_to_shared (page_buffer.c:6951-6984) would rescue a page into the ~519,000-page shared pool, but only if it is fixed 64 times (PGBUF_FIX_COUNT_THRESHOLD, :106) while resident - and Q11 fixes a page 3.47 times per statement - or if a DIFFERENT session's thread touches it. So the misses persist for as long as one connection keeps running the query, and they disappear as further connections arrive: measured Num_data_page_lru1 (the shared hot zone) 15,092 -> 82,352 -> 97,369 while Num_data_page_private_count falls 5,002 -> 1,638 and reads per statement fall 49,292 -> 34,538 -> 18,306 -> 3,519 -> 135 -> 112 over five successive connections.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: PostgreSQL's index scan calls ReadBufferExtended with strategy = NULL (bufmgr.c:926), so PinBuffer takes the default branch and increments usagecount up to BM_MAX_USAGE_COUNT (bufmgr.c:3335-3341), and StrategyGetBuffer runs a clock sweep over the entire NBuffers array (freelist.c:184) with no per-backend or per-session budget of any kind. Q11's ~1.4 GB working set therefore becomes fully resident in the 8192 MB shared_buffers during the first statement and stays resident: every EXPLAIN ANALYZE of Q11 taken in this session, 22 minutes and ~370 statements apart, reports the same `Buffers: shared hit=676275` with `read` absent (zero) and Execution Time 1079.898 ms vs 1080.016 ms. PostgreSQL's small-window mode exists (BAS_BULKREAD, freelist.c:442) but is opt-in for large sequential scans and is not used by an index scan.

There is no per-backend, per-session or per-connection buffer budget anywhere in the file
src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c:926 ReadBufferExtended(reln, forkNum, blockNum, RBM_NORMAL, NULL) - an index scan passes strategy = NULL

src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c:3335-3341 `if (strategy == NULL) { /* Default case: increase usagecount unless already max. */ if (BUF_STATE_GET_USAGECOUNT(buf_state) < BM_MAX_USAGE_COUNT) buf_state += BUF_USAGECOUNT_ONE; }` - with no strategy a page competes for the entire pool and earns full usagecount, so a repeated scan's pages become and stay resident

improvements.priority_justification: Largest single measured effect in the campaign to date and a direct same-engine A/B: CUBRID's Q11 physical page reads per statement fall 566,103 -> 0 and its block median falls 3.544 s -> 1.342 s (2.6408x) with the plan, the query text, every parameter and the page-FIX count all held constant (trace `fetch` 1,012,042 -> 1,011,949, 0.01%). 95% of the recovered time is accounted for by the trace's own fetch_time (2,061 ms -> 326 ms of a 3,360 ms -> 1,532 ms statement). PostgreSQL is at its final level from the first statement (`shared hit=676275 read=0`, Execution Time 1079.898 ms vs 1080.016 ms 22 minutes and ~370 statements later). P0 rather than P1 because the defect also makes single-query performance UNREPRODUCIBLE for an operator: nothing the operator can see or set changes between 3.544 s and 1.342 s, only how many distinct sessions have previously touched the pages.
improvements.q14_evidence: Q14 is a scan-resident stress case for this candidate and measures the retention gap directly on whole-engine /proc IO sampled across every engine PID. Q14's working set exceeds both engines' equal 8192 MB budget (CUBRID lineitem 10,670.9 MiB + part 380.5 MiB; PostgreSQL 8,790 MB + 320 MB), so neither engine can hold it and the question is purely how much each RETAINS between statements. Per measured statement CUBRID issues 431,446 read syscalls moving 7.068 GB -- exactly 16,383 B per call, i.e. one 16 KiB page per miss -- which is a 63.2% miss rate against lineitem's 682,937 heap pages. PostgreSQL over the same regime issues 49,077-84,844 read syscalls for 1.19-1.87 GB. Device reads are ZERO on both sides (the host page cache absorbs everything), so this is not disk latency: it is CPU spent copying pages the engine already read. The cost is visible in the profile as CUBRID's kernel/libc copy band -- rep_movs_alternative 9.61%, __memmove_evex_unaligned_erms 4.46%, filemap_get_read_batch 1.20% = 15.27% of 19.2536 core-s = 2.940 core-s per statement. NOTE for future queries: `cubrid statdump` is UNUSABLE for PER-STATEMENT physical-read accounting on this server -- bracketing one full statement gives delta 0 for Num_data_page_fetches and Num_data_page_ioreads in both -c and non-cumulative mode, and the stage-14.7 diag block recorded delta 0 for every counter while /proc/<cub_server>/io recorded 28.27 GB of rchar over the same four statements. The counters are not permanently stuck (they advanced 2,292,477 across this session) but they do not track statement completion; the update mechanism was NOT determined and no Q14 claim depends on it (q14-statdump-unusable.txt). Q14's buffer evidence therefore rests on /proc/<pid>/io sampled across every engine PID and on PostgreSQL's own pg_statio/EXPLAIN BUFFERS counters.
improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked 1 of 1 new Q11 candidate, and ranked above every existing candidate Q11 touches. The measured bands make the ranking, not judgement: IMP-018 is worth 2.6408x of Q11's wall by direct A/B, while the largest existing candidate Q11 can still see after it is removed is IMP-006 at 32.8% of the remaining page fixes, and the next after that is IMP-009 at 619 ms of 1,532 ms of traced statement time. Explanations that were considered and REJECTED with the number that rejected them: (a) 'the working set exceeds the 8 GB pool' (IMP-002's premise) - the set is 97,400 of 524,288 pages, 18.6%, and the saturated state proves it fits, taking 0 reads; (b) 'CUBRID picked the wrong plan' - forcing PostgreSQL onto CUBRID's sort-based aggregation makes PostgreSQL 1.0787x FASTER, so CUBRID's choice is the better one and F_plan on that anchor is 0.927064x; (c) 'the serial group-by sort' (IMP-015) - /*+ NO_HASH_AGGREGATE */ measures 1.340 s against 1.342 s, F_plan 1.001493x, inside the block band; (d) 'the 0.5f hash-aggregate heuristic' (IMP-016) - Q11's true selectivity is 0.940893 globally and 1.000000 on every early prefix, so HS_REJECT_ALL is correct; (e) 'per-page-fix cost' (IMP-013) - CUBRID spends 1339.0 ns of total query CPU per page fix against PostgreSQL's 1475.2 ns, i.e. it is 1.1017x CHEAPER per fix, so the CPU factor is a fix-COUNT factor (F_work 1.496357x) and not a unit-cost factor; (f) 'a memory-stall difference' - CUBRID's IPC is 1.65 against PostgreSQL's 1.39, i.e. CUBRID stalls LESS.

alternative: Make num_private_chains dynamically settable (system_parameter.c:4168-4175 currently PRM_CLEAR_DYNAMIC_FLAG) so an operator can set it to 0 and disable the private lists. Rejected as the primary direction: it is a workaround for a wrong default and it throws away the private lists' intended many-session benefit instead of sizing it.

Demote rather than victimize an over-quota private page, i.e. move it to a shared LRU instead of recycling it. Recorded as implementation direction (3); it is the structurally cleanest fix and needs no constant at all, but it changes the victim path rather than one arithmetic expression, so it is ranked after the ceiling change.
containment: IMP-002 - the same symptom (physical reads that a correctly-sized pool should not take) but a different premise. IMP-002 is about a working set that EXCEEDS the pool; Q11's is 18.6% of it. IMP-018 is why a set that fits is still not retained. Fixing IMP-018 does not fix IMP-002's Q01/Q03/Q04/Q06 cases and vice versa; Q11 is recorded on IMP-002 as the query that bounds its effect from above.

IMP-007 - what each of those reads COSTS once it happens (a synchronous single-page pread on the query thread). IMP-018 removes the reads, IMP-007 makes them cheaper. On Q11 IMP-018 dominates: it removes 100% of them. IMP-007 should be re-prioritised against whatever survives an IMP-018 fix.

IMP-010 - the same private-LRU machinery seen from the parallel side: there a page READ BY A PARALLEL WORKER never reaches a private list at all because the worker's thread entry has private_lru_index = -1. IMP-010 is 'the private list is bypassed'; IMP-018 is 'the private list is too small'. A fix to either must not regress the other, and Q11 (fully serial) plus Q06 (fully parallel) are the two controls.

IMP-013 - explicitly NOT a Q11 factor: with reads at 0 on both engines the buffer bands are 24.13% (CUBRID) vs 23.72% (PostgreSQL) and CUBRID is cheaper per fix. Q11 is recorded on IMP-013 as a negative control.

improvements.risk: low on correctness, medium on many-session performance (see correctness_risk)
improvements.root_cause_title: A single session's retainable buffer working set is capped at PGBUF_PRIVATE_LRU_MAX_HARD_QUOTA = 5000 BCBs regardless of data_buffer_size, because every page a query reads is placed on that session's PRIVATE LRU list and escapes into the shared pool only when a DIFFERENT session touches it or it reaches 64 fixes while still resident; so an 8192 MB pool retains 78 MiB for one connection, and the SAME query gets 2.6408x faster as later connections migrate its pages out
improvements.upstream_precedent: No prior CBRD issue or PR in the pinned tree at 607f1ee9 changes PGBUF_PRIVATE_LRU_MAX_HARD_QUOTA, MIN_PRIVATE_RATIO or the private->shared promotion rule. The private-LRU quota machinery itself (pgbuf_adjust_quotas, pgbuf_assign_private_lru, the zone thresholds) is the established design being adjusted, so this is a re-parameterisation of an accepted mechanism rather than a new one. On the PostgreSQL side the corresponding decision - no per-backend buffer budget, opt-in BAS_BULKREAD rings only - is ancient and settled; that is a precedent for the design, not for a CUBRID patch.
improvements.validation_criteria: (1) Q01-Q22 results byte-identical - mandatory for any buffer change. (2) On a freshly started server with data_buffer_size=8192M, the FIRST connection running Q11 reaches within 5% of 1.342 s and within 5% of 112 physical reads per statement, measured the same way (/proc/<cub_server>/io syscr delta per statement, cross-checked against trace `ioread`); today the first connection measures 3.544 s and 566,103 reads. (3) The connection-migration curve flattens: the block median of connection 1 and connection 20 agree within the 1.28% Q11 block band, where today they differ by 2.6408x (q11-conn-probe.txt is the before-trace to reproduce against). (4) Num_data_page_private_count is no longer pinned at 5,000-5,003 while a scan whose working set is 18.6% of the pool is running. (5) Q01, Q03, Q04 and Q06 - the queries whose working sets genuinely exceed the pool - are not regressed, since raising the private ceiling changes their victim order too. (6) A concurrency control: N concurrent sessions each scanning a different 18%-of-pool working set must not degrade against the current build, which is the failure mode the adaptive quota guards.

improvements.correctness_risk: None for results: selectivity affects only plan choice and evaluation order, never the row set, and Q12's predicates are a conjunction so any order yields the same rows. The regression risk is plan-shape churn: a changed sarg selectivity also multiplies into QO_NODE selectivity and therefore into join ordering and index choice for other queries, so it must be validated across all of Q01-Q22, not just the query that found it.

improvements.difficulty_reason: The estimator already has everything it needs: both sides are attributes of the same table with histograms already collected under the section 8 statistics contract, and the histogram accessor used by the attribute-vs-constant arm (histogram_get_comp_selectivity) is called two arms away in the same switch. The change is to fill in one empty case with a histogram-overlap estimate and fall back to 0.1 only when either side lacks a histogram. No plan-structure, protocol or data-structure change.
improvements.effect_range: Projection from measured counts and a measured unit cost: 33,243,739 excess term evaluations x 39.1 ns per term evaluation = 1.2998 core-s, 19.2% of Q12's 6.7771 core-s CPU excess and 5.46% of CUBRID's 23.8024 core-s, i.e. about 0.220 s of the 4.039 s median at the measured U=5.89315. The unit cost is the per-term portion of profile band C (eval_pred 8.46% + tp_value_compare_with_error 5.07% + eval_value_rel_cmp 2.90% + mr_cmpval_date 1.01% = 17.44% = 4.1512 core-s over 106,195,014 evaluations); the per-ROW entry point eval_data_filter (1.63%) is deliberately excluded because re-ordering does not change how many rows enter the filter. This is an UPPER bound on the ordering effect alone and does NOT assume attribute materialisation shrinks: heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues runs once per row for all sarg attributes regardless of term order, so IMP-020's band is untouched by this fix and the two must not be summed as if they overlapped.
improvements.evidence_event: Predicate-term evaluations per statement = sum over the evaluation order of the number of rows that REACH each term. Denominator: the prefix survivor counts, each an independent ground-truth count(*) that both engines answer identically (q12-selectivity-probe-cubrid.out vs q12-selectivity-probe-pg.out).
improvements.evidence_type: projection (measured evaluation counts x measured per-evaluation unit cost from a verified-PID profile)
improvements.explanation: CUBRID estimates l_commitdate < l_receiptdate and l_shipdate < l_commitdate at 0.1 each when they actually pass 0.6323 and 0.4876, so it evaluates the two LEAST selective predicates first and the two most selective (l_receiptdate range 0.1517, l_shipmode IN 0.2857) last, performing 106,195,014 term evaluations where the true-selectivity order needs 72,951,275 and PostgreSQL's cost-ordered filter happens to need 91,506,768.
improvements.implementation_direction: Fill in the PC_ATTR/PC_ATTR arm of qo_comp_selectivity() (query_planner.c:10520) with a histogram-overlap estimate for the (attr op attr) case: with both columns' histograms already available under the section 8 contract, P(X < Y) can be estimated by convolving the two bucket distributions, which is the same construction CBRD-26746 already accepted for equi-join selectivity from histograms. Fall back to DEFAULT_COMP_SELECTIVITY only when either side has no histogram. A cheaper interim step that needs no new math: raise the attr-vs-attr default from 0.1 to a value that does not systematically outrank real constant predicates -- PostgreSQL's DEFAULT_INEQ_SEL of 1/3 is the obvious reference point, and on Q12 alone it would already move both terms behind the 0.1517 range predicate and the 0.2857 IN list, recovering the full 33.2M excess evaluations.

measurement.note_the_comparator_is_not_the_problem: Profile band C is 4.5391 core-s on CUBRID against 4.9697 core-s on PostgreSQL, i.e. 0.913x -- CUBRID's per-evaluation cost is 39.1 ns against PostgreSQL's 54.3 ns. CUBRID loses this band on COUNT, not on unit cost, which is why the candidate is an optimizer defect and not an expression-evaluation one.

improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked SECOND of Q12's candidates, behind IMP-020 (19.2% versus 69.5% of the measured CPU excess) but ahead of Q12's IMP-010 relation on addressable size (1.2998 core-s versus the +0.5360 core-s kernel-band delta) and ahead of everything on cost-to-fix: it is one empty switch arm with an accepted upstream precedent for exactly the same construction. It is a PROJECTION rather than a direct A/B because CUBRID offers no switch that changes sarg order without also changing the estimate -- /*+ NO_PARALLEL_SCAN */ and /*+ PARALLEL(n) */ leave the term order untouched -- so the direct A/B requires the patch itself and is recorded as validation criterion (3).

alternative: IMP-020 (reduce the cost of each materialised row rather than the number of predicate evaluations). Disjoint profile bands (C versus A+B); effects add but are not summed against the same core-seconds.
related: IMP-003 - same family: a selectivity ESTIMATE defect that survives because the estimator silently falls back to a constant. IMP-003 is a wrong histogram-derived value for leading-wildcard LIKE; this is a missing estimate entirely, and unlike IMP-003 its damage is to evaluation ORDER rather than to cardinality and join choice.
IMP-014 - also a selectivity-construction defect (multi-column FK match estimated as a product), also optimizer-category, no band overlap.

improvements.root_cause_title: The selectivity of a comparison between two ATTRIBUTES of the same table is an unconditional hardcoded DEFAULT_COMP_SELECTIVITY = 0.1 -- the attribute-vs-attribute arm of qo_comp_selectivity() is an explicit empty '/* TODO: add histogram selectivity */' -- and because qo_discover_edges() then orders sarg terms by ASCENDING estimated selectivity, every column-vs-column comparison is evaluated BEFORE genuinely selective constant predicates, inverting the evaluation order exactly where the estimate is a placeholder
improvements.upstream_precedent: Yes, and directly on point. 10d0aa0e7 [CBRD-26746] 'Use histograms for equi-join selectivity and a significance-based MCV admission test' (#7508) replaced a constant default with a histogram-derived estimate for the attribute-vs-attribute EQUALITY case; this candidate is the same change for the attribute-vs-attribute INEQUALITY case, which #7508 left as the TODO now sitting at query_planner.c:10520. aabba8d1e [CBRD-26202] (#7180) introduced the histogram infrastructure and 5510afbfb [CBRD-27039] (#7442) fixed five histogram-consumption defects, so both the mechanism and the practice of correcting its consumers are established in the pinned tree.

improvements.difficulty_reason: Removing the per-value teardown (band B) is localized -- the sarg attributes of a scan have a fixed domain set per scan, so DB_VALUE containers can be initialised once per scan and reused rather than cleared per row. Removing the materialisation itself (band A) is structural: it requires a lazy or offset-cached attribute path so that a predicate can read an attribute directly out of the page image without constructing a DB_VALUE, which touches heap_attrinfo_*, the mr_data_readval_* type contract and every consumer that assumes a fully built DB_VALUE.
improvements.effect_range: Direct profile attribution: band A +3.2854 core-s and band B +1.4219 core-s, together +4.7073 core-s of Q12's +6.7771 core-s total query CPU excess (69.5%). Upper bound on what a perfect fix could recover is CUBRID's own 9.6923 core-s in those two bands; a realistic first target is band B in full (1.5019 core-s, 6.3% of CUBRID's query CPU) plus the per-row header/domain re-decode inside band A (or_* + tp_domain_disk_size = 7.47% = 1.7780 core-s), i.e. 3.2799 core-s or 13.8% of CUBRID's query CPU, which at the measured U=5.89315 is about 0.557 s of Q12's 4.039 s. No larger wall claim is made: a CPU saving converts to wall only in proportion to utilization.

Denominator: attributes materialised per statement = 5 x 59,986,052 = 299,930,260 on CUBRID (l_orderkey, l_shipdate, l_commitdate, l_receiptdate, l_shipmode) and 15 x 59,986,052 = 899,790,780 on PostgreSQL (slot_deform_heap_tuple must walk attributes 1..15 to reach l_shipmode, which is attribute 15 of lineitem's 16).
improvements.evidence_type: profile attribution (verified PID set, 333,064 samples, 0 unresolved symbols, 89.38% of the profile banded with an empty unbanded remainder)
improvements.explanation: CUBRID spends 27.31 ns of total query CPU per attribute materialised against PostgreSQL's 5.45 ns -- 5.01x -- and then spends a further 1.5019 core-s tearing those values down, against PostgreSQL's 0.0800 core-s, because PostgreSQL never builds a value object in the first place. CUBRID loses this band while materialising THREE TIMES FEWER attributes than PostgreSQL.
improvements.implementation_direction: Two independent steps, cheapest first. (1) Hoist the per-row, per-attribute invariants out of heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues(): a scan's attribute set, their domains and their disk sizes are fixed for the whole scan, so tp_domain_disk_size() and pr_type_from_id() should be resolved once into the HEAP_CACHE_ATTRINFO at scan open, and the DB_VALUE containers initialised once and REUSED, which removes db_value_domain_init()/pr_clear_value() from the per-row path entirely (band B). (2) Give the sarg path an attribute accessor that reads the value in place from the page image for the fixed-width types, so a predicate on a DATE or a CHAR(n) never needs a constructed DB_VALUE. Step (2) is the same direction as the accepted per-row-overhead reductions CBRD-26924 and CBRD-27041 already took for the scan path, extended from page/visibility handling to attribute handling.

measurement.note_on_ipc: CUBRID's IPC is HIGHER (2.32 vs 1.99): it is not stalling, it is executing 1.784x more instructions per row. That excludes a memory-stall explanation for this band and points at instruction count, i.e. work done per row.

It is P0 rather than P1 because the excess is paid on EVERY row of a 59,986,052-row scan whose predicates reject 99.48% of them, i.e. it is paid almost entirely on rows that are then discarded.

So Q14's residual is purely CPU-per-row: 277.17 ns/row (CUBRID) vs 165.04 ns/row (PostgreSQL) of total query CPU. The profile attributes it: CUBRID's row-materialisation + predicate band (heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues 9.64%, eval_pred 8.94%, tp_value_compare_with_error 3.66%, eval_value_rel_cmp 3.03%, or_mvcc_get_header 2.22%, spage_get_record 2.52%, pr_clear_value 1.25%, heap_scan_get_visible_version 2.40% and siblings) is 44.22% of 19.2536 core-s = 8.514 core-s per statement, against PostgreSQL's tts_buffer_heap_getsomeattrs 36.73% + ExecInterpExpr 8.69% and siblings = 60.06% of 9.9003 core-s = 5.946 core-s -- a 1.4318x like-for-like ratio on the same 59,986,052 rows. improvements.root_cause_title: Per-row scan output is materialised into fully-typed DB_VALUEs: for every row the heap scan re-reads the MVCC/representation header, re-resolves each attribute's domain and disk size, calls a type-specific mr_data_readval_* to build a DB_VALUE, and afterwards tears each one down with pr_clear_value -- where PostgreSQL deforms the same tuple into a flat Datum/isnull array using cached attribute offsets, with no per-value type object, no per-value domain init and no per-value teardown at all
improvements.upstream_precedent: Yes, for the direction. a2f738e75 [CBRD-26924] 'Cut per-row overhead in non-fixed heap scan: COPY all-visible shortcut' (#7281) and b334446d6 [CBRD-27041] 'page-copy-then-peek scan' (#7441) are both accepted, and #7441 is IN the pinned build 607f1ee9 (SSOT section 3). Both reduce per-row scan overhead by hoisting work out of the row loop; this candidate applies the same principle to the attribute-materialisation step those two did not touch. No prior CBRD issue or PR was found that caches per-attribute domain or disk-size resolution across rows, or that reuses DB_VALUE containers across scan rows.
improvements.validation_criteria: (1) Q01-Q22 results byte-identical, in particular Q12's 2 rows MAIL 62071/93045 and SHIP 62426/93261 against sink/Q12-cubrid-headline-block1.out; (2) heap_attrinfo_read_dbvalues self-cost falls below 12% of the CUBRID profile on Q12 (from 21.64%) and the band-B symbols below 1.5% (from 6.31%), measured the same way with the same verified-PID perf attachment; (3) CUBRID instructions per lineitem row scanned fall from the measured 2,493 toward PostgreSQL's 1,398, recorded with perf stat over the same 60 s window; (4) Q12 CUBRID median wall improves against 4.039 s under the same warm_establish + measure_block protocol with the WARM gate still CONVERGED; (5) total_query_cpu does not increase.

improvements.correctness_risk: Medium. The change admits plans rather than forcing them, and qexec_groupby_index() is long-standing and already exercised by single-table queries, so no new execution path is introduced. The specific hazard is claiming an ordering across a join type that does not preserve it; validation criterion 5 pins that, and both engines already have the join-type guard written down.

improvements.effect_range: Direct same-engine A/B on CUBRID: 1.5617x (0.883 s -> 1.379 s, medians of 5) on an isolated 1,500,000-group aggregate where the ONLY change is adding one 1-row cross join, which cannot change the grouping work; the plan flips from 'iscan pk_customer_c_custkey (covers)' + '/* ---> skip GROUP BY */' to 'temp(group by)' + 'sort: 1 asc'. An explicit positive index hint cannot recover it (B' 1.371 s, plan text byte-identical to B), which is the runtime confirmation of the admission-time release. PostgreSQL's mirror A/B values the same optimization at 1.7268x (GroupAggregate 523.773 ms vs HashAggregate 904.450 ms over the same Index Only Scan), so the effect is not CUBRID-specific pessimism. On Q13 itself the addressable band is 16.4857% of traced CUBRID wall. NOT additive with IMP-015 or IMP-016.

containment: Distinct from IMP-015: IMP-015 is about the sort-based group-by running single-threaded once it exists; IMP-021 is about the sort never being needed. Fixing IMP-021 removes the workload IMP-015 fails to parallelise, so the two are NOT additive on any query where both fire.

Distinct from IMP-016/IMP-017: those are about hash aggregation being abandoned or mis-parameterised. Q13's inner GROUPBY reports 'hash: partial', i.e. hash aggregation was NOT abandoned here; the cost is the materialisation the plan shape forces around it.
Distinct from IMP-011/IMP-014: those are about choosing the wrong JOIN. Q13's two engines choose the SAME join over the same FK index.

improvements.root_cause_title: A group-by-skip index scan plan is released at birth whenever the query contains a join, because qo_check_plan_on_info() tests index->head->groupby_skip -- a flag that is only ever written later, in qo_top_plan_new(), and only when the final top plan is itself a scan -- where the ORDER BY twin six lines above it tests a candidate predicate instead; so the sort-free streaming GROUP BY is unreachable behind any join and an unconditional SORT_GROUPBY is inserted
improvements.upstream_precedent: Yes, in this very source tree: CBRD-26906, cited in the comment at query_planner.c:9257-9260 ('an interesting-order (group-by / order-by skip) index scan also means the hinted index is usable, so a positive index hint that only provides ordering (no key-range) still suppresses the sequential scan below'). That change taught the planner that an index whose only contribution is ordering is a real alternative on the HINT path; IMP-021 extends the same reasoning to the ADMISSION path. CBRD-24044 is referenced in the adjacent comment at :9274-9275 as the earlier state of the same code.
validation_criteria: Q13's CUBRID estimated plan shows an ordered customer access with '/* ---> skip GROUP BY */' and no 'sort: 1 asc' above the join, and the trace's 20,861 temp pages go to 0.
Result equivalence re-proved by the SSOT section 11 gate: 46 rows, exact ordered match, and the ten ground-truth cardinalities G0-G8 unchanged.
The section 8-c A/B collapses toward 1.0x: 'select c_custkey, count(*) from customer, region where r_regionkey = 0 group by c_custkey' approaches the 0.883 s of the join-free form.
No plan regression on Q01-Q12, re-checked with the estimated-plan harness; the change only admits an alternative.

Left-outer-join null-extension semantics preserved: the ordering is taken from the OUTER (preserved) side only. query_planner.c:12621-12628 already documents the RIGHT-outer restriction the new predicate must respect, exactly as PostgreSQL's build_join_pathkeys() does at pathkeys.c:1303-1306.

improvements.correctness_risk: None to results. This code produces only a cost-model estimate; it cannot change which rows a predicate accepts. The risk is plan churn: making anchored NOT LIKE estimates ~30x larger will reorder sarg terms on any query that mixes one with a more selective predicate, and can flip a join side. That is the intended effect, but it must be re-checked against the Q01-Q22 estimated-plan set.

improvements.explanation: CUBRID scores only the part of the pattern AFTER the first wildcard and assumes a range predicate covers the rest; for NOT LIKE no such range is ever built, so the most selective part of the pattern is simply not counted.
improvements.implementation_direction: (a) MINIMAL: give pattern_heuristic_selectivity() the caller's operator, and when it is PT_NOT_LIKE do not skip the fixed prefix -- score it with FIXED_CHAR_SEL like any other literal. improvements.q16_evidence: Q16 is this candidate's DISCOVERY and ISOLATION query, and it is a clean isolation because the defect fires without changing the plan. alternative: Rejected alternative: raise the [0.0001, 0.9999] clamp at histogram_cl.cpp:1529-1536. It would change the number without fixing the cause -- the estimate would still be identical for 'ZZZZZ%' and 'MEDIUM POLISHED%'. Rejected by the pattern-independence measurement.

Rejected alternative: rewrite NOT LIKE into a NOT(range) so the existing range estimator applies. Larger blast radius (it changes the sarg/term structure and the index-usability decision, not just the estimate) for the same numeric outcome as (b).
containment: SIBLING OF IMP-003, NOT A DUPLICATE. Same file and same outer function (histogram_get_like_selectivity), but IMP-003 is the non-MCV BUCKET-BOUNDARY arm (:1487-1501) on a LEADING-WILDCARD pattern producing an UNDER-estimate of a positive LIKE; IMP-022 is the HEURISTIC PREFIX-SKIP arm (:1311-1337) on an ANCHORED pattern producing an OVER-estimate of the positive LIKE and therefore an UNDER-estimate of NOT LIKE. Q16 exhibits both at once on two different columns, which is what separates them: s_comment's leading-wildcard LIKE lands on the 0.0001 lower clamp (IMP-003) in the same statement in which p_type's anchored NOT LIKE lands on the 0.9999 upper clamp (IMP-022). Fixing either does not fix the other; their effects are NOT additive on any single term because no term takes both branches.

Distinct from IMP-019 (attribute-vs-attribute comparison defaults to 0.1): that is a missing estimator arm for a different operator class. The shared consequence -- a placeholder estimate reaching qo_discover_edges()'s evaluation-order sort -- is the reason both are exposed, but the code and the operators are disjoint.

Distinct from IMP-004: IMP-004 is the RUNTIME cost of the UTF-8 LIKE matcher; IMP-022 is the PLAN-TIME estimate of how many rows will reach it. Q16 measures both, and they must not be summed: fixing IMP-022 changes how often the matcher runs on some other query, fixing IMP-004 changes what each run costs.

CBRD-26667 (the authorization bypass added at histogram_cl.cpp:1582-1586 and schema_template.c:1997) shows the same histogram path is under active maintenance in this SHA.

improvements.difficulty_reason: Sub-item (a) -- do not build a list file when the group-by sort already orders the input by the DISTINCT operand -- is a localized early-return of exactly the shape PostgreSQL's aggpresorted flag implements, and CUBRID already has the sort-list machinery to extend the group-by sort key (qexec_groupby's SORT_LIST). Sub-item (b) -- an in-memory dedup below a size threshold instead of a qfile -- is also local (qdata_process_distinct_or_sort is 45 lines). Sub-item (c) -- parallelising the post-sort finalize loop -- is structural and is NOT proposed here.
improvements.effect_range: Addressable band on Q16 = the serial-phase differential, 1.041 - 0.291 = 0.750 s of 2.886 s (25.99%) against the plan-controlled PostgreSQL leg, plus whatever part of the 2.6666 core-s band A exceeds PostgreSQL's 2.1036. Sub-item (a) (recognise that the group-by sort can carry the DISTINCT key, PostgreSQL's aggpresorted) is bounded ABOVE by PostgreSQL's own measurement of the same optimization on this query -- which is NEGATIVE here (-7.60%), so (a) is NOT the right first fix on Q16 and is recorded as such. Sub-item (b) (in-memory per-group dedup instead of a qfile) is the one Q16 supports: it targets the 27,840 file open/sort/destroy cycles and the 1,186,602 malloc+serialize+append operations, which is where band A and the serial phase both sit. Lower bound 0.750 s (the measured serial differential), upper bound 1.041 s (the whole serial phase).
improvements.evidence_event: Rows entering the grouping/DISTINCT pipeline, and the wall time of the sub-1.5-active-unit phase of each measured statement. Denominator: one Q16 statement = 1,186,602 rows into 27,840 groups (42.62 rows per group), a count both engines answer identically as exact ground truth.
improvements.explanation: CUBRID pays a file open, a per-row malloc+serialize+append and a full external sort per group to compute a distinct count; PostgreSQL pays one equality call per row, or at worst an in-memory per-group tuplesort, inside the pipeline.
improvements.implementation_direction: (a) CONDITIONALLY SKIP THE FILE WHEN THE INPUT IS ALREADY ORDERED BY THE OPERAND: PostgreSQL's aggpresorted, i.e. extend the SORT_GROUP_BY sort list with the DISTINCT operand and replace the per-group file with a single compare-against-previous. Q16 measures the SHAPE half of this as worth -7.60% on PostgreSQL, so this is a code-simplification/allocation win, not a sort win, and must not be sold as the latter. (b) THE Q16-SUPPORTED FIX: in qdata_process_distinct_or_sort() (query_aggregate.cpp:70-115), use an in-memory hash/sorted set for a group until it exceeds a budget and only then fall back to qfile_open_list(). Q16's groups average 42.62 rows and the widest is bounded by the 100,000-row supplier cardinality, so essentially every Q16 group fits trivially. This removes 27,840 file open/destroy cycles, 27,840 qfile_sort_list() calls and the 1,186,602 pr_data_writeval_disk_size/db_private_alloc/data_writeval/qfile_add_item_to_list/db_private_free sequences per statement. (c) FOR COUNT SPECIFICALLY: qdata_finalize_aggregate_list() at :1428-1431 only needs list_id_p->tuple_cnt, so PT_COUNT DISTINCT never needs an ordered result -- a counting hash set is sufficient and does not need the sort at all. (d) NOT PROPOSED HERE: parallelising the post-sort finalize loop. It is the largest single lever (1.041 s at ~1 unit) but it is a structural change to qexec_groupby's phase split, and (b)+(c) shrink the same phase without it.

src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c:8019 gather_grouping_paths() -- for reference on why PostgreSQL's finalize is not a serial tail: the sort sits BELOW the Gather Merge, so the leader's aggregate loop overlaps the workers.
improvements.priority_justification: 1.041 s of every 2.886 s Q16 CUBRID statement (35.9% of the busy window) runs at fewer than 1.5 active units, against 0.291 s for the PLAN-CONTROLLED PostgreSQL leg doing the identical 27,840 per-group dedups -- a 3.5773x ratio on the serial phase alone. Profile band A (list-file / sort / group-by) is 2.6666 core-s per CUBRID statement against 2.1036 for PostgreSQL native and the whole of Q16's residual after F_plan is F_cpu 3.031730x on F_work exactly 1.000000x.
improvements.q16_evidence: Q16 is this candidate's DISCOVERY query and supplies its isolating experiment. The experiment is unusual and worth stating precisely: it uses PostgreSQL's own enable_presorted_aggregate switch to force PostgreSQL into CUBRID's aggregation shape, which both anchors F_plan (0.929368x) and produces a plan-controlled cross-engine pair in which the ONLY remaining difference is how each engine implements per-group DISTINCT. On that pair CUBRID spends 9.492891 core-s per statement against 3.131179 (F_cpu 3.031730x) on F_work exactly 1.000000x, and 1.041 s of its 2.886 s runs below 1.5 active units against 0.291 s (3.5773x). The CUBRID trace localises the same 1.17 s as the gap between GROUPBY's total 1,471 ms and the 291-306 ms its three sort workers spend, and /proc IO shows 0 physical reads, so it is pure CPU in the post-sort finalize loop -- exactly where qdata_evaluate_aggregate_list() serializes 1,186,602 operands into per-group list files and qdata_finalize_aggregate_list() sorts 27,840 of them with duplicate elimination.
improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked 1st of the five candidates carrying Q16 evidence. It is the only one with a direct same-engine A/B bounding its band (the F_plan anchor plus the serial/parallel phase split), and it owns the largest measured differential: 0.750 s of the 1.689 s Q16 gap (44.4%) sits in the serial-phase difference alone. IMP-008 (predicate evaluation, 1.5901 vs 0.2695 core-s) and IMP-020 (row materialisation, 1.1809 vs 0.1751) own larger CPU RATIOS but are attributed by profile bands, not by an A/B, and both are already measured on four earlier queries. IMP-004 (LIKE matcher, 0.8202 vs 0.0264 core-s) is third. IMP-022 is ranked last of the new work because its measured Q16 wall effect is zero. Effects must NOT be summed: band A (IMP-023), band D (IMP-008), band E (IMP-020) and band C (IMP-004) are disjoint self-% partitions of the same profile, but IMP-023's serial-phase differential and its band-A share describe the SAME work from two directions and overlap.

alternative: Rejected explanation, with the number that rejected it: 'CUBRID's per-group DISTINCT plan shape is the wrong shape.' PostgreSQL's own enable_presorted_aggregate A/B on the identical plan says the opposite -- the per-group shape is 1.075998x FASTER for PostgreSQL than the presorted shape its optimizer picks (1.112363 s vs 1.196902 s). The shape is fine; the implementation of the shape is not.

Rejected explanation: 'the group-by sort is not parallelised' (IMP-015). The Q16 trace shows 'GROUPBY ... (parallel workers: 3)' in BOTH the native and the NO_PARALLEL_SCAN run, so sort_check_parallelism() admitted it. Rejected by the trace.

Rejected explanation: 'hash aggregation was abandoned' (IMP-016/IMP-017). The plan is 'hash: false, sort: true' and PostgreSQL independently costs GroupAggregate below HashAggregate on the same query. Rejected by both engines agreeing.

Rejected explanation: 'CUBRID is short of buffer memory / is re-reading pages' (IMP-002/IMP-007/IMP-018). /proc/<cub_server>/io moves 14,912 bytes of rchar and 0 read_bytes across a whole four-statement block. Rejected by 0 physical reads.

Rejected explanation: 'CUBRID's parallelism is worse'. F_units is 0.855774x, i.e. CUBRID runs at MORE active units than PostgreSQL (3.28929 vs 2.81489), and its own NO_PARALLEL_SCAN A/B gives 2.6646x speedup at 81.0% efficiency. Rejected by the units measurement.
containment: Distinct from IMP-006, which owns list-file materialisation of INTERMEDIATE JOIN RESULTS (qexec_end_one_iteration -> qfile_generate_tuple_into_list). IMP-023's list files are created by qdata_process_distinct_or_sort() once per GROUP and hold aggregate OPERANDS, not join output. The two share qfile_* symbols in the profile and their bands must NOT be summed on any query where both fire; on Q16 band A is reported as one band for exactly that reason.

Distinct from IMP-015: IMP-015 is the group-by SORT refusing to parallelise. On Q16 the sort DID parallelise (3 workers) and the cost is in the serial post-sort finalize loop. Fixing IMP-015 would not touch Q16's serial phase.

Distinct from IMP-021: IMP-021 removes the group-by sort entirely by admitting an ordered index scan. On a query where both applied the effects would overlap (IMP-021 removes the input IMP-023's loop consumes), so they are NOT additive.
Sub-item (a) is bounded by, and on Q16 CONTRADICTED by, the F_plan anchor; only sub-items (b) and (c) carry Q16's measured band.

improvements.root_cause_title: count(DISTINCT x) under a sort-based GROUP BY is executed as one temporary LIST FILE PER GROUP: every operand row is converted to its disk representation and appended to that group's file, and at each group boundary the file is sorted with duplicate elimination just to read back its tuple count -- and the whole per-row/per-group loop runs SINGLE-THREADED after the parallel sort phase, where PostgreSQL either dedups adjacent rows with one equality call or runs an in-memory per-group tuplesort inside the pipelined GroupAggregate
improvements.upstream_precedent: Yes on the PostgreSQL side, as a direct model: PostgreSQL 16 added exactly this optimization for its own per-group-tuplesort implementation (adjust_group_pathkeys_for_groupagg() at planner.c:3501, the aggpresorted flag, EEOP_AGG_PRESORTED_DISTINCT_SINGLE at execExpr.c:3916 and the enable_presorted_aggregate GUC), which is what makes it a known-good design rather than a speculative one -- and Q16's A/B on that very switch is what measures its worth. On the CUBRID side the closest in-tree precedent is the MIN/MAX early-out already present in the same function (query_aggregate.cpp:76-81, 'since max(distinct a) == max(a), handle these without distinct processing'), i.e. the codebase already accepts special-casing a DISTINCT aggregate that does not need the file. No CBRD issue for the per-group list file itself was found in this SHA.
validation_criteria: Q16 CUBRID serial phase (sub-1.5-active-unit time per statement, measured with actual sample timestamp deltas) falls from 1.041 s toward PostgreSQL-nopresorted's 0.291 s; the headline median falls from 2.886000 s accordingly.

The CUBRID trace's GROUPBY total time falls toward the ~300 ms its three sort workers already spend, i.e. 'GROUPBY (time: 1471 ... parallel workers: 3, time: 291..306)' loses the ~1,170 ms gap between the two numbers.
Profile band A falls from 2.6666 core-s per statement, and lf_freelist_claim + lf_freelist_retire + lf_stack_pop (3.73% combined, the 27,840-file churn) drop out of the top-40 flat profile.
Q16 result equivalence re-proved by the SSOT section 11 gate: 27,840 rows, exact ordered match on all four output columns, supplier_cnt values unchanged.

A wide-group regression case (a DISTINCT over a single group with >1e6 distinct values) must still complete and must not exceed the configured memory budget -- this is the criterion that proves the spill path survived.
No regression on Q01-Q15's committed headline medians beyond their recorded block-to-block bands.

q17_dedup_note: Q17 allocated NO new IMP ID. The ledger was synced and searched by root-cause title, CUBRID source location, PostgreSQL source location and mechanism before deciding; every measured CUBRID-side effect matched an existing root cause, so per SSOT section 18 the existing entries received Q17 relations and evidence rather than a duplicate ID. next_id remains IMP-024. Two candidate hypotheses were raised during Q17 and REJECTED BY MEASUREMENT rather than filed: (1) 'the subquery cache is one entry from the subquery_cache.c:378-383 disable cliff at SF10' -- rejected because a probe with 16,030 distinct keys, 7.8x Q17's 2,044, still reported status=enabled under the same 2 MB default, and the traced size that motivated the hypothesis is itself inflated by IMP-005; (2) 'CUBRID takes zero data-page fetches on Q17' -- rejected because a statdump delta taken with adequate flush latency shows +161,531 fetches and +1 ioread per execution, so the zero deltas seen around the 0.59 s block were a statistics-flush-latency artifact. Q17's largest engineering finding is a PostgreSQL weakness (no memo for a correlated SubPlan at src/backend/executor/nodeSubplan.c:198-241, against CUBRID's sq_get/sq_put at src/query/fetch.c:4086-4111, plus an unparallelisable join at src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c:931-950 and :960-973) and is recorded in reports/Q17/report.md sections 7-8 rather than in this ledger, which allocates CUBRID improvement candidates.
q18_dedup_note: Q18 allocated NO new improvement ID. Searched the ledger by title, CUBRID source location, PostgreSQL source location and root cause before considering allocation. Q18's dominant finding (63.4% of block wall at one active unit during a sort-based GROUP BY) is IMP-015's existing root cause at external_sort.c sort_check_parallelism(), so Q18 was added as a relation with new evidence plus a measured rejection of one of that entry's own alternatives. The spill-size finding belongs to the existing IMP-016/IMP-017 aggregation-memory root cause. One genuinely NEW CUBRID/PostgreSQL asymmetry was found and deliberately NOT allocated: src/parser/type_checking.c:5037 adds PT_DISTINCT to every IN-subquery unconditionally where PostgreSQL proves the subquery already distinct at analyzejoins.c:1372-1389 (query_is_distinct_for) and reduces SEMI to an inner join. Its measured Q18 effect is +0.188% (34.570999 s vs 34.505999 s, direct same-engine A/B), which is about one within-block sd and inside the 1.6% error band, because Q18's DISTINCT runs AFTER the HAVING filter on 624 rows. SSOT section 18 requires a candidate to state an evidence event and denominator that actually moved, so it is recorded in the Q18 report's section 7 source contrast with an explicit 'no measured effect on Q18' instead of being allocated an ID from evidence that does not support one.
